P0D00.d: Some battery types can give off gases while charging; for that case the conductive charging standards provide a state in which the vehicle asks the station for ventilation. The vehicle signals it by switching a much smaller resistor of about 270 Ω onto the pilot, which drags the level to around 3 V; the station then only delivers power where ventilation is assured.
s: Stored code, charging usually still works
Charging system warning in the cluster
c: Open control wire or loose connector of the ventilation switch circuit
Ventilation switch or its resistor branch open inside the module
Failed driver stage in the charging control module

P0D01.d: The ventilation switch lets the vehicle request charging state D, in which a small resistor pulls the pilot down to about 3 V and the station may only deliver power with ventilation. P0D01 means this switch does not produce a plausible pilot level.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Charging possibly refused at stations without ventilation
c: Internal fault in the VICM/charging module switching or measuring circuit
Ventilation resistor branch out of tolerance or high contact resistance
Leakage on the pilot line, for example moisture in the charge inlet

P0D02.d: P0D02 marks the control or feedback line of the ventilation switch as too low, usually a harness wire grounded somewhere along its route or a charging module driver that has failed shorted. That switch places a resistor of about 270 Ω across the pilot so that the level falls to roughly 3 V, the state in which a vehicle demands charging with ventilation.
s: Charging refused at stations without ventilation
Stored code without noticeable effect
c: Ventilation switch control or feedback wire shorted to ground
Shorted driver stage in the charging control module
Corrosion in a connector bridging the line to ground

P0D03.d: Here the line that drives or reports the ventilation switch reads above its valid range, which points to a short to a supply voltage or a driver stage that no longer switches. The ventilation switch is the vehicle-side element that requests charging with ventilation by loading the control pilot with roughly 270 Ω and lowering it to around 3 V.
s: Stored code, sometimes with a charging system warning
Charging refused if the switch is forced closed
c: Ventilation switch control or feedback wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the charging module no longer switching
Lost ground at the switch letting the line float high

P0D04.d: P0D04 covers short, irregular disturbances in the ventilation switch circuit: the signal drops out or flickers, while lasting faults would be stored as P0D00, P0D02 or P0D03. Worn or corroded contacts in the charge inlet or module connector, and wires that lose contact under vibration, are the obvious suspects.
s: Charging sessions stop without obvious reason
Code returns after clearing
c: Loose or spread terminal in the ventilation switch circuit
Corrosion or moisture in the charge inlet or module connector
Chafed wire with contact loss under vibration

P0D05.d: Stuck Off for the ventilation switch means the module commands the switch closed, yet the pilot does not drop to the level around 3 V that marks a request for charging with ventilation. Possible causes are a switch that no longer closes, an open resistor in the roughly 270 Ω branch, or a measuring fault in the module.
s: Stored code, charging normally still possible
Charging system warning in the cluster on some vehicles
c: Ventilation switch in the module no longer closing
Open resistor or solder joint in the ventilation branch
Pilot measuring fault in the charging module

P0D06.d: Stuck On means the ventilation switch remains closed when it should be open, so the pilot is held near 3 V and the station reads a permanent demand for charging with ventilation. Stations that cannot provide ventilation do not supply power in that state, which in practice stops charging altogether.
s: Charging station does not supply power
Charging error message after plugging in
c: Ventilation switch contacts welded or sticking closed
Short across the ventilation resistor branch
Module output or software holding the switch on

P0D07.d: P0D07 is the general circuit code for positive contactor A of the charging system, the switch that joins the plus side of a charging path to the traction battery. Depending on the design this path comes from the DC fast-charge inlet or from the on-board charger; the Chevrolet Volt, for instance, places charging contactors between charger and pack.
s: Charging not possible or aborted
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor

P0D08.d: P0D08 means positive charging contactor A has stayed closed although the control module commanded it open, typically because the contacts have welded. The module notices this when voltage remains on the charging side, for instance at the charge port once a session has ended, as a Toyota patent on charge-relay sticking explains.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
Charging refused
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode
c: Contactor contacts welded, for example after switching under load
Battery module software misjudging the contactor state (GM Lyriq, Ram ProMaster EV bulletins)
Driver stage or coil supply that does not switch off

P0D09.d: P0D09 is set when positive charging contactor A fails to close: after the command the expected voltage never shows up on the charger side. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (VICM 2016, HPC2 2019): during charger precharge, with charging and precharge contactors on and the negative main contactor still off, a charger voltage under 10 V ends the test; 2016 needs 8 failing samples out of 9, 2019 waits for at
s: Charging does not start or ends shortly after plugging in
Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Charging or high-voltage warning in the cluster
c: Contactor mechanically failing to close or burnt contacts
Fault in the on-board charger or integrated charging unit (Kia ICCU bulletin)
Control software needing an update (Stellantis, GM Lyriq)
Missing coil supply because of a wiring or fuse fault

P0D0A.d: P0D0A covers the drive circuit of positive charging contactor A: the module compares the commanded state of its driver with the voltage and current it actually sees on the coil line. GM spells this out for the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR: with the driver off, an output above 4 V means an open line and one close to supply voltage a short to power; with the driver on, coil current below 57 mA (Volt 2019: 194 mA) al
s: Malfunction indicator lamp (GM Type A or B)
Vehicle does not charge
c: Open or high-resistance coil control wire or connector
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty high-side driver in the control module

P0D0B.d: P0D0B reports that the control circuit of positive charging contactor A works electrically but does not behave plausibly – coil current or line voltage outside the window expected for the commanded state, or a response that comes too slowly. No manufacturer documents P0D0B publicly.
s: Charging sessions fail sporadically
Stored code, possibly with a charging system warning
c: Contact resistance or corrosion in the control circuit connectors
Weakening driver stage in the control module

P0D0C.d: P0D0C stands for a control line of positive charging contactor A that reads too low, usually a short to ground or a driver output pulled down. When the coil is fed through a high-side driver, a grounded line leaves the contactor without power or overloads the driver.
s: Charging does not start
Charging system warning
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector creating a path to ground

P0D0D.d: P0D0D means the control line of positive charging contactor A sits too high, typically from a short to a supply voltage or a driver that no longer switches off. The coil may then stay energised, so the contactor could close without a command, which the module has to prevent.
s: Charging blocked
Charging or high-voltage system warning
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open ground return of the coil letting the line float high

P0D0E.d: P0D0E is the general circuit code for negative contactor A of the charging system, which connects the minus side of the charging path – from DC inlet or on-board charger – to the traction battery. It is used when the module sees an electrical fault on that contactor that it does not classify more precisely.
s: Charging not possible or aborted
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor

P0D0F.d: P0D0F flags negative charging contactor A as stuck closed: it still conducts after the open command, usually through welded contacts or a misjudged state. Ford stores it in the BECM of the 2021–2022 Mustang Mach-E together with main-contactor codes such as P0AA1 and P0AA4; bulletins 22-2178 and 23-2020 replace the high-voltage battery junction box and reprogram the BECM, and a flat 12 V battery or the Stop Safely Now
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or wrench lamp
Stop Safely Now message or no ready mode (Ford)
Discharged 12 V battery
c: Faulty high-voltage battery junction box with the charging contactors (Ford Mach-E)
Battery module software misjudging the contactor (Stellantis 4xe, GM Lyriq)

P0D10.d: P0D10 means negative charging contactor A does not close when told to, so the charging path never gets its return line and the session fails. Ford names it in the BECM of the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E next to main-contactor codes; the bulletins (23-2020, 23-2257) replace the high-voltage battery junction box and update the BECM.
s: Charging does not start or stops
Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
Vehicle may not start (Lyriq, Stellantis)
c: Faulty high-voltage battery junction box with the charging contactors (Ford Mach-E)
Battery module software needing an update (GM Lyriq, Stellantis)
Contactor failing to close or burnt contacts

P0D11.d: P0D11 is the open-circuit and driver check for negative charging contactor A. GM uses it on the Chevrolet Volt (2011, 2014) and the Cadillac ELR: the module compares the commanded driver state with what the line shows; with the driver off, an output above 4 V (2011: 2 V) means open and one close to supply voltage a short to power, and with the driver on a coil current below 57 mA is judged open as well.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Vehicle does not charge
c: Open or high-resistance coil control wire or connector
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty driver stage in the control module

P0D12.d: P0D12 points to a control circuit of negative charging contactor A that is electrically intact yet implausible: current, voltage or switching response do not fit the command. No manufacturer documents P0D12 publicly.
s: Charging sessions fail sporadically
Stored code, possibly with a charging system warning
c: Contact resistance or corrosion in the control circuit connectors
Poor ground of the control module or coil return

P0D13.d: P0D13 means the control line of negative charging contactor A reads too low, which points to a short to ground or a driver output held down. The coil then receives no current, or too little, and the contactor stays open.
s: Vehicle refuses to charge
Charging system warning
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector creating a path to ground

P0D14.d: P0D14 is set when the control line of negative charging contactor A reads too high, for example through a short to the 12 V supply or a driver stage that will not switch off. That can keep the coil energised and the contactor closed without a command, so the module blocks charging.
s: Charging blocked
Charging or high-voltage system warning
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open ground return of the coil letting the line float high

P0D15.d: P0D15 reports an open high-voltage interlock loop in charging system A. This low-voltage loop runs through the connectors and covers of the charging path – inlet, charger and their HV leads – and breaks as soon as one of them is unplugged, so the module can keep that path de-energised.
s: AC charging not possible
Charge inlet light indicates a fault
c: HV connector in the charging path not fully seated or latched (Volvo XC40)
Broken interlock wire or pushed-back terminal
Missing or loose cover on a charging component

P0D16.d: P0D16 flags a charging interlock loop that delivers a signal, just not the one expected – for example a reading that fails to follow when the module switches its test source on and off. No manufacturer documents P0D16 publicly.
s: Charging refused
Charging system warning
c: Contact resistance or corrosion in an interlock connector
HV connector in the charging path inserted only partway
Fault in the module's interlock source or measuring stage

P0D17.d: P0D17 means the sensed voltage of the charging HVIL loop is too low. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (2011, 2014) and the Cadillac ELR: while the module sources 5 V into the loop, a sensed value under 30 % of the reference in two samples out of two at 12.5 ms sets the code as Type A, with the MIL on after one trip.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Charging refused
c: Interlock wire chafed and touching ground
Moisture or dirt in an interlock connector causing leakage
Fault in the interlock source or measuring circuit of the control module

P0D18.d: P0D18 flags a charging HVIL signal that sits too high. On the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR GM tests the loop in two states: with the 5 V source off, a sensed level above 24 % of reference (5 of 6 samples in 2011, 5 of 8 for 2014 and ELR), and with it on, a level above 44 % (4 of 6), set the code as Type A, MIL after one trip.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp (GM Type A)
Propulsion or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Slow or no AC charging
c: High resistance or partial break in the interlock loop
Battery module software needing an update (Polestar 2)
Faulty integrated charging unit (Kia Niro EV ICCU)
Interlock wire shorted to a voltage source

P0D19.d: P0D19 covers a charging interlock loop that drops out and comes back, so the signal flips between valid and invalid within a short time. Loose terminals, a connector that is not fully latched, a chafing wire that only touches over bumps and vibration-sensitive solder joints are typical causes.
s: Charging stops unexpectedly
Intermittent charging system warning
c: Loose or spread terminal in an interlock connector
HV connector in the charging path not fully latched
Chafed interlock wire making contact only under vibration

P0D1A.d: P0D1A flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of coolant control valve B, a second actuator in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. Which physical valve gets the letter B, and what it switches, is up to the vehicle maker.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced charging or drive power because battery temperature cannot be managed
c: Broken wire or corroded connector in the valve B drive circuit
Open coil or motor winding inside valve B
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P0D1B.d: P0D1B is stored when coolant control valve B of the battery loop is electrically intact but fails to reach or hold the position the controller asks for, or stays in its off state. How a maker judges this varies: for valve A, GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt learns the end stops, expects the target within 1.5 s and watches for drift above 3 %, while Audi and Toyota infer a wrong valve state from coolant temperatures.
s: MIL or battery thermal system warning
Battery temperature rises during fast charging or hard driving
Charging or drive power limited
c: Valve B mechanically stiff or blocked by debris
Worn valve actuator that no longer reaches its target
Diagnostic limits in the module software set too tightly
Low coolant or trapped air distorting the temperature-based check

P0D1C.d: P0D1C means coolant control valve B of the battery circuit remains in its active position although the controller has commanded a change. What active means depends on the design: on valve A, Mercedes hybrid battery management distinguishes a shutoff valve that will not close (P0CE000) from one that will not open (P0CE100), which shows that makers map on and off to opposite valve states.
s: MIL or battery thermal system warning
Battery warms slowly in cold weather or charging is slower than usual
c: Valve B jammed in its active position
Output stage or supply that keeps the valve energised
Module software misjudging the temperature response of the loop

P0D1D.d: P0D1D reports that the drive line of coolant control valve B reads too low, which normally means a short to ground. No manufacturer publishes P0D1D itself.
s: MIL after two trips (where the maker uses a two-trip code)
Battery cooling or heating restricted, charging or power limited
c: Valve B driver wire chafed and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve motor

P0D1E.d: P0D1E is the short-to-voltage counterpart for coolant control valve B: the controller sees its drive line high at a moment when it should be low. P0D1E is not described in any public manufacturer document.
s: MIL after two trips (where the maker uses a two-trip code)
Battery thermal management in fallback mode, charging or power limited
c: Valve B driver wire pinched against a supply line
Output stage in the controlling module stuck high
Damaged or contaminated connector bridging two pins

P0D1F.d: P0D1F says a control module could not align its internal date and time with the reference the rest of the vehicle uses. Hybrid modules need a trustworthy clock because several checks depend on how long the car has been parked: CARB, for example, ties cold-start monitoring to at least six hours off, and GM separately checks its module power-off timer against the on-timer (P262B, more than 5.6 % deviation on the 2012 V
s: Check engine light without a noticeable driving fault
Code returns as a variant after a software update until the car has slept
c: Module software misdetecting the time comparison (Volvo BECM software 2.11)
Timers not yet resynchronised after programming because the car has not slept
Missing or wrong time information from the module providing the reference clock

P0D20.d: P0D20 concerns the on-board charger in its constant-voltage phase, typically near the end of a charge, when it should hold its high-voltage output at a set value. The code means the measured output voltage strays too far from that target.
s: Charging stops early or the battery does not reach its target level
MIL and charging system message
c: Fault in the charger's power stage or voltage control
Charge control software in the hybrid control module

P0D21.d: P0D21 is set when the high-voltage output of the on-board charger stays below what the controller expects. GM's Volt and ELR tables split the test in two: during normal charging the charger bus must not fall under 150 V, and when the charger only powers the battery heater, the bus must reach at least 75 % of an expected value calculated from charger current times 70 ohms.
s: Vehicle does not charge
MIL, often after two charging trips
Battery not preheated while plugged in during cold weather
c: Failing power stage inside the charger
High resistance or fault in the charger's high-voltage output path or heater load

P0D22.d: P0D22 means the on-board charger does not deliver the high-voltage current it was asked for. GM's Volt compares actual and desired current in constant-current mode against a table: 150 of 300 samples set it in 2011, One Trip Type A; from 2014 a second part also catches a charger that was switched on, with more than 201 V commanded, but never enabled its output after 6 s.
s: Vehicle does not charge or charging stops
MIL on after a charge session ends
Problem shows mainly on AC level 2 stations
c: Charge control software in the hybrid or battery control module (GM PIP bulletins)
Internal fault in the on-board charger

P0D23.d: P0D23 points to a short on the high-voltage output side of the on-board charger. GM runs this check while the charger contactor is only in its precharge state and the multi-purpose contactor is open, a moment when almost no current should flow on the charger bus.
s: Charging refused immediately after plugging in
MIL on at once
c: Internal short in the charger's high-voltage output stage
Damaged high-voltage cable between charger and battery
Charging contactor path conducting when it should not

P0D24.d: P0D24 is stored when the on-board charger reports an internal temperature above its permitted limit. Chargers protect themselves by reducing power or stopping, so the driver typically notices slow or interrupted AC charging.
s: AC charging slow, interrupted or impossible while DC fast charging works
Warning message for the electric system, sometimes MIL
c: Internal defect in the charger or charging control unit (Kia ICCU replacement)
Low coolant, failed pump or blocked air flow on the charger cooling path
Charger temperature sensor reading too high

P0D25.d: P0D25 is about the precharge of the charger's high-voltage bus, the short phase before the charging contactors close in which the bus capacitance is brought up to battery voltage through a limiting path. The code means this voltage arrived sooner than physically plausible.
s: Charging refused at the start of a session
Charging system warning
c: Charging contactor welded or closing too early
Bus or pack voltage sensor reporting wrong values
Bus capacitance much lower than expected

P0D26.d: P0D26 means the charger's high-voltage bus did not come up to battery voltage within the allowed precharge time. GM's Volt 2011 to 2015 and ELR 2014 to 2016 require the bus to sit within 5 % of pack voltage for 0.25 s before 10 s have passed; the 2016 and 2017 Volt allow only 0.700 s to reach 95 % (later 95 to 105 %); all are One Trip Type A.
s: Vehicle does not charge on 120 V or 240 V
MIL on at once
With a blown disconnect fuse, loss of propulsion
c: Open precharge resistor, fuse or contactor in the precharge path
Blown fuse in the manual service disconnect (Bolt EV bulletin)
Erratic proximity signal from a wet or corroded charge port

P0D27.d: P0D27 says the AC voltage reaching the on-board charger sits lower than the charger accepts while charging is permitted. Unlike most charger codes, the cause often lies outside the car.
s: AC charging does not start or stops
House circuit breaker trips when plugging in
MIL
c: Weak or overloaded AC supply at the charging location
Damaged wiring or loose contact between charge inlet and charger

P0D28.d: P0D28 is the mirror case of P0D27: the AC voltage at the charger input lies above the range the charger can accept. Mitsubishi evaluates both on the Outlander PHEV while the PHEV-ECU allows charging; the charger then stops and the technician works from the outside in, beginning with the supply and the charging cable, then the wiring between inlet and charger, and only last the charger.
s: AC charging stops or does not start
Code found in memory without any complaint
c: Input voltage sensing inside the charger reading too high
Charger software storing the code without a real fault (Audi ghost DTC)
Actual overvoltage or unstable supply at the charging location

P0D29.d: P0D29 is set when the on-board charger draws less AC current than expected for the power it was asked to deliver, while voltage and charging permission are present. No manufacturer documents P0D29 publicly.
s: AC charging much slower than usual
Charging stops or charging system warning
c: Charger power stage not ramping up
High resistance at the charge inlet, cable or plug contacts
Input current sensor reading too low
Charging station or cable limiting current more than signalled

P0D2A.d: P0D2A reports that the on-board charger draws more AC input current than allowed. GM's Volt and ELR use two limits: more than 17 A at 185 V or above, more than 13 A below 185 V; 240 failures in 300 samples set it as One Trip Type A.
s: AC charging stops shortly after starting
MIL on
On-board charging inoperative while DC charging may still work
c: Fault in the charger's input or PFC stage (Toyota/Lexus charger replacement)
Charger or powertrain module software (Stellantis, Ford bulletins)
Input current sensor reading too high

P0D2B.d: P0D2B concerns the driver circuit of the control pilot indicator, a lamp or LED with which the vehicle signals the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. The code covers the lamp's own wiring, not the pilot signal itself.
s: Indicator stays dark or lit regardless of charging state
MIL, depending on model after one or two trips
c: Damaged wiring or loose connector to the indicator
Faulty LED driver in the controlling module

P0D2C.d: P0D2C is set for a fault in the driver circuit of charge status indicator A, the light that tells the driver whether the car is charging. On the Chevrolet Volt that light is part of the diagnosis itself: bulletin PIP4905E has technicians watch whether the charge indicator on the instrument panel stays steady green.
s: Charge status light dark or permanently lit
MIL, depending on model after one or two trips
c: Broken wire or corroded connector to the indicator
Faulty LED driver in the controlling module

P0D2D.d: Drive motor A's inverter measures the DC link voltage it switches, and voltage sensor A is the channel that passes this value to the motor controller. P0D2D is the general circuit fault for that channel: the signal is missing or electrically unusable, without a more specific low or high verdict.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Vehicle does not become ready to drive or electric drive is reduced
No start after charging and remote start (Mach-E)
c: Inverter or powertrain module software fault (Ford 21B02)
Loose connector or damaged signal wiring of the voltage sensor
Voltage sensing circuit inside the inverter failed

P0D2E.d: P0D2E means the inverter voltage reading of drive motor A is electrically valid but disagrees with other measurements of the same high-voltage bus. Mitsubishi shows the logic for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with voltage control active, the power drive unit compares capacitor 1 with the rear motor unit and with both channels of capacitor 2; a gap of 100 V or 50 V held for 0.2 s sets the code, and an implausible PWM perio
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Engine will not start, only electric driving possible (Mercedes)
Reduced drive power
c: Voltage sensing in the power drive unit drifts or reads wrong
Fault in another HV component, e.g. belt starter-alternator (Mercedes)
High resistance or loose high-voltage connection between modules

P0D2F.d: P0D2F reports that the signal of inverter voltage sensor A for drive motor A sits at the bottom of its range, typical of an open circuit, a short to ground or no high voltage at all. In the 2018 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi sets it in the front motor control unit when the sensor output stays below 0.5 V, equal to about 10 V on the bus, for 0.3 s while the propulsion system is active.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Vehicle not ready to drive or electric drive unavailable
c: Blown high-voltage fuse or disconnected HV cable
Voltage sensing in the power drive unit failed (open or short to ground)

P0D30.d: P0D30 is the high-side partner of P0D2F: the inverter voltage signal of drive motor A stays near its upper limit. Mitsubishi checks it on the 2018 Outlander PHEV with the front motor unit supplied at 8 to 16 V; a sensor output above 4.7 V, which stands for roughly 440 V, for 0.3 s sets the code.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electric drive switched off or reduced
c: Voltage sensing in the power drive unit shorted to supply
Real overvoltage from battery or HV circuit (both motor units report)

P0D31.d: P0D31 covers a voltage signal from the drive motor A inverter that drops out or jumps for brief moments without staying out of range long enough for P0D2F or P0D30. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning that comes and goes
Brief power loss or jerky electric drive
c: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Chafed signal wiring with intermittent contact
Sensing circuit in the power electronics fails with heat or vibration

P0D32.d: P0D32 means DC/DC converter A, which supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery, has become too hot. Unlike the sensor codes P0C38-P0C3C, the reading itself is trusted; the temperature is the problem.
s: Several warning lights including MIL
Reduced hybrid system performance
12 V battery discharges, charging warning
c: Coolant loss in the power electronics circuit, e.g. damaged PCU radiator (Honda)
Weak electronics coolant pump or air in the cooling circuit
Internal converter fault with excess heat

P0D33.d: P0D33 says the DC/DC converter carries more current than its limit. The converter links the high-voltage or 48 V system with the 12 V network; an internal short in the power stage, a shorted 12 V cable or consumer, or a failed output stage can push the current beyond what the converter accepts, and it then switches off to protect itself.
s: Charging system fault message
12 V battery not charged, later no start
Electrical consumers switched off
c: Internal circuit board fault in the converter (Land Rover MHEV)
Short in a 12 V cable or consumer on the converter output
Damaged high-voltage or 48 V supply cable

P0D34.d: P0D34 is the general code for the current flowing through the high-voltage battery system as a whole. The pack current sensor codes P0ABF-P0AC3 judge the sensor signal; this group judges whether the current itself fits the operating state.
s: Hybrid system warning or MIL
Reduced electric power or charging restrictions
c: Battery current sensor reads wrong but within range
Unexpected current path in the HV system (contactor, consumer)

P0D35.d: P0D35 flags a battery system current that swings more than the operating state explains, for example rapid changes while the requested power is steady. No manufacturer publishes set conditions for this code.
s: Hybrid system warning, possibly intermittent
Power reduction or jerky electric drive
c: Loose high-voltage connection or chattering contactor
Current sensor or its wiring with intermittent signal

P0D36.d: P0D36 means the battery system delivers or accepts less current than the controller expects for the power it commanded. No manufacturer documents a threshold publicly.
s: Reduced electric power and regeneration
Slow charging
Hybrid system warning or MIL
c: High resistance in the HV path or contactor not closing properly
Current sensor stuck at a plausible but too low value
Aged battery pack with high internal resistance

P0D37.d: P0D37 records excessive current in the high-voltage battery system. Mitsubishi describes it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the PHEV-ECU watches the HV circuit for overcurrent whenever the car is ready or charging.
s: EV or hybrid system warning, with MIL on some makes
High-voltage system switches off, car not ready or not charging
c: Short or fault in an HV component (charger, DC/DC, A/C, inverter)
Contactor points damaged by the overcurrent (junction box)
Hybrid control unit or battery fault (code returns)

P0D38.d: P0D38 is the general circuit code for the sensor that measures the AC current entering battery charger A, the on-board charger. It sets when the signal is missing or electrically invalid; range, low, high and intermittent faults have their own codes P0D39-P0D3C.
s: AC charging does not start or stops
Charging fault indication on the dashboard or charge port
c: Current sensing inside the on-board charger failed
Open or shorted sensor wiring or connector
Charger software or supply voltage fault

P0D39.d: P0D39 flags an implausible reading from the sensor that measures alternating current at the input of charger A, the on-board charger. Both documented users test its zero point.
s: AC charging does not start
MIL on (GM)
Charging fault shown at the charge port or in the cluster
c: Zero point of the current sensor inside the charger has drifted
Measuring electronics of the on-board charger failed

P0D3A.d: P0D3A is the low-signal fault of the charger A input current sensor. Mitsubishi defines it for the 2022 Outlander PHEV as a short to ground: if the sensor output falls below 0.344 V, which corresponds to roughly -54 A, for 0.5 s while the charger supply is 10-16 V, charging is stopped and the combined charger and DC/DC unit is swapped.
s: AC charging stops or never begins
MIL on (GM)
c: Current sensor signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Unstable 12 V supply to the charger module

P0D3B.d: P0D3B reports that the charger A input current sensor reads too high. On the 2022 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi interprets a sensor voltage above 4.658 V, equivalent to more than about 54 A, lasting 0.5 s as a short to the supply side; charging ends and the integrated charger/DC-DC unit is the listed part.
s: AC charging quits shortly after plugging in
MIL on (GM)
c: Current sensor signal shorted to supply voltage inside the charger
Genuine overcurrent at the charger input from an internal short

P0D3C.d: P0D3C covers a charger A input current signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Volt and Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV, which use the neighbouring codes P0D39-P0D3B, list no intermittent variant.
s: Charging stops at random and may restart
Charge sessions take longer than usual
c: Loose or corroded connector at the on-board charger
Current measuring element inside the charger failing

P0D3D.d: P0D3D is the basic circuit code for voltage sensor A at the input of charger A, which measures the AC supply voltage arriving from the charge inlet. It stands for a missing or electrically invalid signal; plausibility, low, high and sporadic faults have their own codes P0D3E-P0D41.
s: AC charging is refused
Charging fault indication
c: Open or shorted voltage sense circuit in the charger
Damaged AC wiring between charge inlet and charger

P0D3E.d: P0D3E means the AC input voltage seen by the on-board charger does not agree with other information. GM uses it across generations: the 2011-2014 Volt charger module compares the AC peak voltage with two internal bulk voltage readings and sets a Type A fault when both differ by more than 34 V (59 V in 2014); the 2016 and 2019 Volt check the charger's duty-cycle report while driving and fail it outside 8-12 %, Type B.
s: Charge incomplete or interrupted
MIL on (GM)
Problem appears only at certain charging stations
c: Charger module software reacting to certain charging stations (GM BCCM update)
Charging station or cord with unusual behaviour, quick re-plugging
Voltage measurement inside the on-board charger faulty
Faulty duty-cycle signal line between charger and controller (2016-2019 Volt)

P0D3F.d: P0D3F reports that the charger's AC input voltage reading is too low. In the 2011-2014 Volt GM's charger module sets it when the AC peak stays below 90 V while AC is present (1.5 s in 2011, 5.5 s in 2014), Type A; the 2016-2019 Volt instead watches a duty-cycle signal at or below 8 %.
s: Charging does not start or is interrupted
MIL on (GM)
Charge cord LEDs flash or the charge indicator changes colour repeatedly
c: Weak, interrupted or noisy AC supply (brown-out, shared circuit)
DC-only adapter used on an AC charger (GM PIT6353)
Charger module software needs update (GM PIC5803D)
Voltage sensor signal shorted to ground in the charger

P0D40.d: P0D40 is the high-signal fault of the charger's input voltage sensor. GM's Volt charger module (2011 and 2014 tables) sets it when the measured AC peak exceeds 422 V for 160 of 200 ms and lights the MIL as a Type A fault; in the 2016 and 2019 Volt the controller reads a duty-cycle signal and fails it at 92 % and above or at a constant 0 %, Type B over two trips.
s: AC charging is refused
MIL on (GM)
c: Voltage sensor signal shorted to supply inside the charger
Open duty-cycle signal line between charger and controller (2016-2019 Volt)

P0D41.d: P0D41 is reserved for an input voltage sensor A signal at charger A that is intermittent or erratic, i.e. it jumps or drops out briefly.
s: Charging stops and restarts unpredictably
Fault appears only at one charging location
c: Electrical noise or poor grounding on the AC supply
Loose contact between charge inlet and charger
Voltage measurement in the charger degrading

P0D42.d: P0D42 is the circuit code for the sensor that measures voltage at the 14 V output of the battery charger, a low-voltage DC stage built into the on-board charger and distinct from the vehicle's main DC/DC converter. GM's charger module in the Volt and ELR has such an output and monitors its voltage with P0D43-P0D45, yet no manufacturer publishes P0D42 itself.
s: 12 V battery discharges while the car is plugged in
Charging is interrupted
c: Open or shorted voltage sense circuit of the charger's low-voltage stage
Poor 12 V or ground connection at the charger

P0D43.d: P0D43 says the voltage reported for the charger's 14 V output does not fit other measurements of the low-voltage system. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR compares the reading with the run/crank signal voltage and with the voltage of a further enable line (HVEMB); a difference of 6 V or more for 4 of 5 s stores a Type A fault with MIL.
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging interrupted or not completed
c: Low-voltage sense circuit inside the charger reads wrong
Poor ground or 12 V feed at the charger skews the comparison

P0D44.d: P0D44 is logged once the voltage sensor of the charger's 14 V output delivers an implausibly low raw value. In GM's charger module for the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR the limit is a sensor signal of 1.87 V or less, held for 400 of 500 ms while the low-voltage section is awake; it is a Type A fault and lights the MIL.
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging may stop or not complete
c: Voltage sense signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Failed low-voltage stage of the on-board charger
14 V output collapsed by an external short or overload

P0D45.d: P0D45 is stored when the charger's 14 V output voltage sensor reads too high. GM's battery charger control module in the Volt and ELR fails it at a reading of 16.88 V or above for 400 of 500 ms; the 2011 table rates it Type A, the 2014 table Type B, meaning the MIL comes on only after two consecutive trips.
s: MIL on (GM, after two trips in later model years)
Charging may stop
c: Voltage sense signal shorted to a higher potential inside the charger
Charger low-voltage stage regulating too high

P0D46.d: P0D46 stands for a sporadic or unstable signal from the voltage sensor at the 14 V output of the on-board charger. No manufacturer documents it publicly.
s: 12 V battery not kept charged while plugged in
Occasional charging interruptions
c: Loose 12 V, ground or signal connection at the charger
Voltage sense circuit inside the charger failing intermittently
Electrical interference on the low-voltage network

P0D47.d: P0D47 is the general circuit code for the current sensor in the charger's 14 V output, the measurement of how much current the charger's internal low-voltage stage delivers. No manufacturer publishes this code; GM's Volt and ELR charger module measures the same current but reports only low and high readings (P0D49, P0D4A), with 54 A as its upper limit.
s: 12 V battery discharges during long charging sessions
Charging may be interrupted
c: Open or shorted current sense circuit of the low-voltage stage
Damaged 12 V output connector at the charger

P0D48.d: P0D48 marks a current reading at the charger's 14 V output that lies within its electrical range but makes no sense in context. No manufacturer documents P0D48.
s: Charging fault indication
12 V support during charging reduced or switched off
c: Current sense circuit inside the charger has drifted
Failed low-voltage stage of the charger

P0D49.d: P0D49 reports that the current sensor in the charger's 14 V output reads too low. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR sets it when the raw current value is 0.293 A or less for 400 of 500 ms while the low-voltage section is awake, as a Type A fault with MIL; the 2016 ELR charger table also lists it as a precondition for its output power checks.
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging may fail
c: Open or grounded current sense path inside the charger
Failed low-voltage stage of the on-board charger
12 V supply or fuse of the charger interrupted

P0D4A.d: P0D4A sets when the current sensor in the charger's 14 V output reports 54 A or more. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR applies that threshold for 400 of 500 ms with the low-voltage section awake and treats the result as a Type A fault with MIL.
s: Vehicle will not charge
MIL on (GM)
c: Current sense signal stuck high inside the charger
Overload or short on the charger's low-voltage output

P0D4B.d: P0D4B covers an erratic or intermittent signal from the current sensor in the battery charger's 14 V output. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM's Volt and ELR charger module uses only the low and high codes P0D49 and P0D4A for this measurement.
s: Charging interrupts now and then
12 V battery voltage fluctuates while plugged in
c: Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the charger
Intermittent contact in the charger's current sense circuit
Electrical interference on the low-voltage network

P0D4C.d: P0D4C is the general circuit code for the sensor that reports the DC voltage the on-board charger delivers to the high-voltage traction battery. No manufacturer documents P0D4C publicly; GM (Volt, ELR) and Mitsubishi (Outlander PHEV) split electrical faults of this measurement into the low and high codes P0D4E and P0D4F instead, and GM's Volt checks plausibility with P0D4D.
s: Plug-in charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
Vehicle can still be driven on stored energy or fuel
c: Voltage sensing electronics inside the on-board charger failed
Interrupted signal path or poor internal connection in the charger
Charger software fault, fixed by reprogramming

P0D4D.d: P0D4D means the charger's output voltage reading is electrically valid but fails to match the rest of the system. GM's second-generation Volt (2016-2019 tables) compares it with the traction battery voltage while charging is ready: a gap of more than 30 V sets the code, in 2019 after 320 of 400 samples taken every 25 ms, as a Type B fault with MIL after two trips.
s: MIL on (GM Volt, Bolt)
Slow AC charging or no AC charging
Check electric vehicle system message (Kia)
c: Output voltage measurement inside the charger drifted or inaccurate
Integrated charging unit failed (Kia ICCU, GM charger module)
Reference value from the battery voltage measurement wrong

P0D4E.d: P0D4E reports a signal below the valid range for the sensor measuring the charger's DC output toward the traction battery. In GM's charger module for the 2011-2014 Volt and ELR the raw value must stay at or below 2.62 V for 400 of 500 ms; the fault is Type A and lights the MIL at once.
s: Charging stops or does not start
MIL on (GM)
Charging fault message
c: Voltage sensor signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Internal reference supply of the measuring circuit missing

P0D4F.d: P0D4F is the high-side fault of the charger's output voltage sensor: the reading climbs beyond anything the battery could actually present. GM's 2011-2014 charger module for the Volt and ELR flags a decoded value of 482 V or more for 400 of 500 ms as a Type A fault with immediate MIL.
s: AC charging refused
MIL on (GM)
Charging interrupted with fault message
c: Voltage sensor signal shorted to a supply voltage inside the charger
Measuring stage of the on-board charger failed

P0D50.d: P0D50 stands for an unsteady output voltage signal from the on-board charger: the value jumps or drops out briefly instead of following the slowly changing battery voltage. No manufacturer documents P0D50 publicly.
s: Charging repeatedly interrupted
Charge time noticeably longer than usual
Sporadic charging system warning
c: Loose contact or cracked solder joint in the charger's measuring path
Electrical interference from the charger's power stage
Ageing voltage sensing electronics in the charger

P0D51.d: P0D51 covers a circuit fault of the sensor that measures the direct current the on-board charger pushes into the traction battery. No manufacturer documents P0D51 itself.
s: AC charging does not start
Charging system warning shown
Driving not affected
c: Current sensor or its evaluation circuit in the charger failed
Open signal path between sensor and charger controller

P0D52.d: P0D52 flags an output current reading that lies inside the sensor's range yet cannot be right. Mitsubishi documents the check for the 2022 Outlander PHEV as a zero-point test: while the PHEV-ECU has not granted charging, no current should leave the charger, so an absolute reading of 1.5 A or more lasting 1 s sets the code; charging is halted and the charger/DC-DC unit is replaced.
s: Poor or no AC charging
MIL or electric system warning (Kia)
DC fast charging may still work (Kia)
c: Zero point of the output current sensor has drifted
Charger or integrated charging unit (Kia ICCU) failed

P0D53.d: P0D53 is set when the charger's output current sensor reports a value below its valid floor. GM's charger module in the 2011 and 2014 Volt and the ELR uses a decoded current of 0.098 A or less, present for 400 of 500 ms with the low- and high-voltage sections awake; the fault is Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip, and the power checks P0D5C and P1ECE stay disabled while it is active.
s: Charging stops or never begins
MIL on (GM)
Charging fault indicated at the charge port or in the cluster
c: Current sensor output shorted to ground inside the charger
Supply of the current sensor missing

P0D54.d: P0D54 marks a current reading at the charger's high-voltage output that exceeds the sensor's upper limit. The limit sits well above normal charging current, so the value counts as an electrical fault rather than real current.
s: AC charging interrupted or refused
MIL on (GM)
Charge level stays unchanged after plugging in
c: Current sensor output shorted to supply voltage in the charger
Sensor output stuck at its upper end

P0D55.d: P0D55 describes an output current signal from the charger that flickers, jumps or briefly drops out rather than tracking the regulated charging current. No manufacturer documents P0D55 publicly.
s: Charging pauses and resumes repeatedly
Charging takes much longer than usual
Occasional charging system warning
c: Intermittent contact in the current measuring path of the charger
Solder joints fatigued by charging heat cycles
Switching noise coupling into the sensor signal

P0D56.d: P0D56 is the general circuit fault of proximity detection circuit A, the line through which the vehicle notices that a charging plug sits in its inlet. Under SAE J1772 this proximity pin runs to protective earth through resistors in the plug and a switch tied to the latch button, so the car can block driving away and end charging before the plug is pulled; under IEC 62196 a resistor on the same pin also codes the cab
s: Charging does not start although the cable is plugged in
Vehicle refuses to drive or shows the cable as connected without a plug
Charging system warning
c: Damaged or corroded proximity contact in the charge inlet
Open or chafed wire between charge inlet and evaluating module
Evaluation input in the charger or control module failed

P0D57.d: P0D57 means the plug-present signal of proximity circuit A is electrically within limits but its value or behaviour does not fit the situation, for instance a level between the defined states for plugged, unplugged and latch pressed. FCA uses the code on the Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid: bulletins 08-044-20 (2017) and 08-042-20 (2018) list P0D57 with control pilot codes P0CF3 and P0CF4 behind an illuminated MIL a
s: MIL on (FCA)
Charging starts unreliably or not at all
Plug status shown incorrectly
c: Hybrid control software needs update (FCA HCP/AHCP)
Worn or contaminated proximity contact shifts the resistance
Charging cable or adapter with off-standard proximity resistor

P0D58.d: P0D58 reports a voltage on proximity circuit A that is too low while no plug can possibly be inserted. GM's Volt checks this in its hybrid control processor: in 2011 with the charge door closed or above 12.4 mph in a range other than Park, from 2016 above 20 km/h outside Park, the signal must sit in a window, and less than 4.2 V for 30 of 50 samples (later 240 of 400) sets the code as a Type A fault with immediate MI
s: MIL on (GM)
Vehicle will not start or shift because a plug appears connected
High-voltage battery cannot be charged
c: Proximity signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against body
Loose low-voltage connector at the on-board charger (smart)
Moisture or contamination bridging the inlet contacts
Evaluation input of the control module failed

P0D59.d: P0D59 is logged when proximity circuit A shows a voltage above its expected resting level at a moment when the charge port must be empty. GM's Volt uses the same plausibility window as for P0D58 but trips above 4.8 V: in 2011 with the door shut or above 12.4 mph in a range other than Park, from 2016 at more than 20 km/h outside Park, over 30 of 50 or 240 of 400 samples; the fault is Type A and turns on the MIL.
s: MIL on (GM)
Inserted charging plug not recognised, no charging
Start-up problems after charging (smart)
c: Proximity signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Interrupted ground or reference path of the detection circuit
Loose connector at the charger or charge inlet

P0D5A.d: P0D5A points to a proximity signal on circuit A that flips between states or jumps erratically, so the vehicle sees the plug come and go although nobody touched it. No manufacturer documents P0D5A publicly.
s: Charging aborts sporadically
Plug status message appears and disappears
Occasional refusal to drive off
c: Loose contact in the inlet or at the charger connector
Worn latch switch or contacts in the charging plug

P0D5B.d: P0D5B checks whether the power leaving the charger's built-in 14 V output is physically possible. GM's charger module for the Volt and ELR multiplies the measured 14 V output voltage and current and compares the product with the AC input power times a factor of about 2 plus an offset: 2.5 W in the 2011 table, 125 W in the 2014 Volt/ELR and 2016 ELR tables.
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging interrupted
12 V battery not supported while plugged in
c: Voltage or current measurement of the 14 V stage reads too high
AC input power measured too low
Low-voltage stage of the on-board charger faulty

P0D5C.d: P0D5C judges the power the charger feeds into the traction battery against what it draws from the grid. GM's first-generation Volt and ELR charger module calculates high-voltage output power and flags it when it exceeds AC input power times about 2 plus 30 W (2011) or 120 W (2014 and 2016 ELR), for 1.6 of 2 s, Type A.
s: MIL on after a charging session
Charging slower than expected
Charging interrupted
c: Power stage of the charger degraded, efficiency too low
Module software miscalculates power (Ford SOBDM update)
Output voltage/current or AC input measurement inaccurate
Insufficient cooling of the power electronics during charging

P0D5D.d: P0D5D concerns the active discharge of the charger's high-voltage side after charging ends: the stored voltage collapses faster than the circuit design allows. No manufacturer documents P0D5D publicly; GM's Volt only publishes the opposite case P0D5E.
s: Charging system warning after the end of charging
Next charging session may not start
No noticeable effect while driving
c: Discharge switch inside the charger stuck closed
Charger voltage measurement reads falsely low

P0D5E.d: P0D5E means the high-voltage side of the charger did not drop to a safe level in time after it was disconnected. GM's 2011 Volt charger module fails the test if 60 V or more remain 1.5 s after the discharge command, or 6.75 s after a confirmed communication loss with the hybrid controller; a backup routine then checks for battery current that would reveal a stuck contactor.
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging blocked after the fault
Further high-voltage codes such as contactor faults may be stored
c: Active discharge circuit of the charger not working
High-voltage contactor stuck closed keeps the bus energised
Lost communication between charger and hybrid controller
Charger voltage sensor reads falsely high

P0D5F.d: Where a traction battery is cooled by two fans, each one can report its actual speed back to the controller on a separate sense line. P0D5F is the general circuit code for that return path of fan 2: the line is open or delivers nothing the controller can evaluate.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Reduced electric assist or charging power when the battery warms up
Often no noticeable change while fan 2 still runs
c: Broken feedback wire or terminal pushed out at the fan 2 connector
Corroded or loose connector between fan 2 and the battery controller
Speed signal output inside the fan 2 motor electronics failed
Feedback input of the battery control module defective

P0D60.d: P0D60 means the feedback of battery cooling fan 2 is electrically present but does not fit what the fan was told to do. Volkswagen documents it for the 2014 Touareg Hybrid: the battery controller reads the fan 2 feedback as a voltage and flags this code when it crosses a limit that moves with the commanded duty, somewhere between 1.37 and 3.43 V; fan 1 is judged the same way under P0BC8.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Fan noise that is louder, rougher or weaker than usual
Battery temperature rises faster and electric power is limited
c: Fan 2 runs off its commanded speed due to worn bearing or debris on the impeller
Clogged intake grille, filter or duct of the battery cooling air
Drifting speed feedback stage in the fan electronics
High resistance in the feedback or supply connection of fan 2

P0D61.d: P0D61 reports that the feedback signal of battery cooling fan 2 sits at or near zero. In Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid the battery controller sets it once the fan 2 feedback voltage drops below 0.1 V; the matching fan 1 code is P0BC9.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Fan 2 audibly silent although battery cooling is requested
Reduced electric power, especially in warm conditions
c: Fan 2 feedback wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Fan 2 without supply (fuse, relay or supply wire), so no signal is generated
Feedback output of the fan 2 electronics failed low or motor seized
Feedback input of the battery control module defective

P0D62.d: P0D62 is set when the feedback of battery cooling fan 2 rises above its plausible maximum. Volkswagen gives the threshold for the 2014 Touareg Hybrid as a fan 2 feedback voltage above 3.45 V, mirroring P0BCA for fan 1.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric power limited when the battery gets warm
Fan 2 may still run normally
c: Fan 2 feedback wire shorted to a supply or neighbouring signal
Open ground at fan 2 letting the feedback line float high
Fan 2 electronics stuck at their upper feedback level
Feedback input of the battery control module defective

P0D63.d: P0D63 flags a feedback signal from battery cooling fan 2 that drops out or jumps in steps no spinning fan could produce. The typical culprit is a loose pin or cracked wire that opens and closes with vibration, or interference coupled into the feedback line.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Occasional short phases of reduced electric power
Often no noticeable change in fan operation
c: Loose or spread terminal in the fan 2 feedback connector
Cracked feedback wire that opens under vibration
Electrical interference from nearby high-current or high-voltage wiring
Unstable feedback stage in the fan 2 electronics

P0D64.d: Besides its speed command, a battery cooling fan can have a separate enable line that switches the fan electronics on. P0D64 means the controller has found this enable output open.
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan does not run
Reduced electric assist when the battery gets hot
c: Broken enable wire between battery controller and fan
Fan connector unplugged or not latched, often after battery or trim work
Open enable input inside the fan electronics
Enable driver in the battery system module defective

P0D65.d: P0D65 reports a short to ground on the enable output of the battery cooling fan: the line stays low even though the controller is trying to switch the fan on. GM's 2013 eAssist mild hybrid table 13OBDG05C detects it from the output driver's fault flag for the power pack fan, 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B.
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan never switches on
Engine runs more and electric assist drops in hot weather
c: Enable wire chafed and shorted to body ground
Shorted enable input inside the fan electronics
Moisture or corrosion bridging the enable pin to ground
Enable driver in the battery controller defective

P0D66.d: P0D66 stands for a short to voltage on the enable output of the battery cooling fan. Because the line is pulled high from outside, the fan may run although the controller wants it off, or the controller simply loses authority over it.
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan runs continuously, even with the vehicle off
Discharged 12 V battery after standing
c: Enable wire rubbed through and touching a 12 V supply wire
Moisture in the fan connector bridging enable and supply pins
Internal fault in the fan electronics feeding voltage back onto the enable line
Enable driver in the battery controller defective

P0D67.d: P0D67 says that the control electronics of the on-board charger are not working properly. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV manuals (2019 and 2022) spell out what that means there: with the charger supplied at 10 to 16 V, the code sets when one of its internal supply rails leaves its window for 1 s, 3.0 to 3.6 V for the 3.3 V rail, 5.3 to 6.8 V for the 6 V rail or 9.4 to 14.9 V for the 12 V rail.
s: Plug-in charging stops or does not start
Electric vehicle system warning in the cluster, possibly MIL
Vehicle can still be driven on stored energy or fuel
c: Internal low-voltage supply of the on-board charger out of tolerance
On-board charger or integrated charging unit failed
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger
Charger software fault, fixed by an update where available

P0D68.d: An electric A/C compressor in a hybrid or EV runs its motor from the high-voltage battery through an inverter in the compressor housing, and a sensor there measures the incoming high voltage. P0D68 is the general circuit code for that sensor: its signal is missing or unusable as a whole, without a specific low or high reading.
s: Air conditioning does not cool
Warning message or warning light, depending on the vehicle
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
c: Voltage measurement inside the electric compressor's inverter failed
Compressor reports its sensor value over a faulty data link
Poor high-voltage connection at the compressor

P0D69.d: P0D69 is a plausibility check: the high voltage that the electric A/C compressor measures at its input should match the traction battery voltage, since both see the same supply. GM's Volt sets it when the two differ by more than 15 V in the 2011 table (35 of 40 samples at 250 ms) and by more than 30 V in the 2016 and 2019 tables (8 of 10 s in 2019), each Type B with MIL after two trips and only with contactors closed
s: Check engine light
Air conditioning weak or switched off
Often no other noticeable change
c: Drifting high-voltage measurement inside the electric compressor
Fault on the data bus that carries the compressor voltage value
Hybrid or vehicle controller misjudging the comparison
Error in the battery voltage measurement used as reference

P0D6A.d: P0D6A means the electric A/C compressor reports an input voltage higher than the high-voltage system can actually deliver. GM's 2011 Volt table sets it at 450 V or more (30 of 60 samples at 50 ms); the 2016 and 2019 Volt tables use more than 527.25 V, judged by the compressor itself and sent over the data bus (2019: 4 of 5 s).
s: Check engine light
Air conditioning stops cooling
Driving otherwise normal
c: Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reading too high
Hybrid controller or data link fault

P0D6B.d: P0D6B reports that the high-voltage input reading of the electric A/C compressor sits below the plausible range. GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 ELR set it at 190 V or less in 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms, checked only with the contactors closed for over a second and fault-free.
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM) or immediately (Mitsubishi 2023)
Air conditioning stops cooling
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be restricted
c: Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reads too low
Faulty data link between compressor and hybrid controller (named by Mitsubishi)
Hybrid or vehicle controller evaluates the value incorrectly

P0D6C.d: P0D6C covers a voltage-sensor signal from the electric A/C compressor that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong: single readings outside the expected window or abrupt steps that do not last long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0D6C publicly.
s: Air conditioning cools intermittently
Code returns sporadically after clearing
Often no warning light
c: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the compressor
Intermittent fault on the compressor's inverter board
Marginal high-voltage contact at the compressor connector

P0D6D.d: P0D6D concerns the high voltage actually reaching the electric A/C compressor motor rather than the sensor circuit: the supply is too low to run it. Mazda documents it for the CX-90 PHEV (2024–2026) and CX-70 PHEV (2025–2026) in bulletin 07-002/26: an overcurrent can short the compressor internally and blow the A/C high-voltage fuse, after which the PCM stores P0D6D, often with U0605.
s: Air conditioning does not cool at all
Further codes such as lost communication with the compressor
High-voltage battery may not charge (cable fault)
c: Internal short in the compressor that has blown the A/C high-voltage fuse (Mazda)
Broken high-voltage cable in the supply path (Bentley, battery to on-board charger)
Open A/C fuse or poor high-voltage connection without a compressor defect

P0D6E.d: P0D6E means the high voltage supplied to the electric A/C compressor motor is above what the compressor is built to accept, as opposed to a sensor circuit reading too high (P0D6A). No manufacturer documents P0D6E publicly.
s: Air conditioning switches off
Possibly further high-voltage codes
Warning message depending on the vehicle
c: Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reads too high
Voltage spikes on the high-voltage bus during charging or regeneration
Charger or DC/DC converter regulating the bus voltage incorrectly

P0D6F.d: P0D6F flags excessive current drawn by the electric A/C compressor on its high-voltage DC link while the motor is running. GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR set it when the DC link current exceeds 27 A in 30 of 60 samples taken every 50 ms with a compressor speed request above zero; it is Type B, MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning cuts out under load
Unusual noise from the compressor
c: Shorted winding in the compressor motor
Refrigerant overcharge or excessive high-side pressure
Failing power stage in the compressor inverter

P0D70.d: The control electronics inside an electric A/C compressor carry a temperature sensor on the processor board, called internal sensor A; the compressor uses it to protect itself and reports the value to the vehicle. P0D70 is the general circuit code for it: the value is missing or invalid without a defined low or high reading.
s: Air conditioning weak or off
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
Warning depending on the vehicle
c: Temperature sensor or its circuit on the compressor board failed
Value not transmitted correctly over the data link
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the compressor electronics

P0D71.d: P0D71 is a plausibility test for the compressor control module's internal (CPU) temperature sensor: after a long rest, every temperature in the compressor should be close to its surroundings. GM's 2011 Volt compares it with intake air and with the output-stage sensor and fails above 6 °C in 35 of 40 samples at 250 ms.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in A/C operation
c: Drifting internal temperature sensor in the compressor electronics
Outside air, intake air or IGBT sensor used for comparison is wrong
Compressor not fully cooled down when the test ran

P0D72.d: P0D72 is the high-signal circuit code for the compressor module's internal temperature sensor. With the usual NTC thermistor a high signal means the reading looks extremely cold, and that is how GM defines it: every Volt and ELR table from 2011 to 2019 sets it when the reported CPU temperature is below −40 °C.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning limited or switched off
c: Open circuit in the internal temperature sensor path
Cracked solder joint on the compressor electronics board
Faulty value transmission to the host controller

P0D73.d: P0D73 is the low-signal circuit code for the internal (CPU) temperature sensor of the compressor control module. For an NTC sensor a low signal corresponds to an implausibly hot reading.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning reduced or switched off
c: Short circuit in the internal temperature sensor path
Real overheating of the compressor electronics
Faulty value transmission to the host controller

P0D74.d: P0D74 reports an unsteady signal from the internal temperature sensor of the A/C compressor control module: the reading jumps or drops out in short bursts rather than sitting at one wrong value. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P0D74.
s: Air conditioning cuts out now and then
Code appears sporadically
c: Cold or cracked solder joint on the compressor board
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the compressor
Electrical interference on the sensor signal

P0D75.d: The output driver temperature sensor watches the power transistors (IGBTs) that switch the three motor phases of an electric A/C compressor; they heat up under load, and the compressor reduces speed or stops before they overheat. P0D75 is the general circuit code for this sensor without a defined low or high value.
s: Air conditioning switched off
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
c: Temperature sensor at the IGBT module or its circuit failed
Sensor value not transmitted correctly to the vehicle
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the compressor electronics

P0D76.d: P0D76 checks whether the compressor's output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor agrees with other temperatures after a cold soak. GM's 2011 Volt fails it when the IGBT reading differs from outside air by more than 11 °C and from the CPU sensor by more than 7 °C after the compressor has been off for over 21,600 s, with coolant and outside air within 15 °C of each other; 35 of 40 samples at 250 ms.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in A/C operation
c: Drifting IGBT temperature sensor in the compressor inverter
Outside air or CPU temperature used for comparison is wrong
Power stage still warm when the test ran

P0D77.d: P0D77 is the high-signal circuit code of the output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor in the electric A/C compressor. As with an NTC sensor, the high signal shows up as an impossibly cold temperature: GM sets it when the IGBT reading is at or below −40 °C, in all Volt and ELR tables from 2011 to 2019.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning switched off
c: Open circuit in the IGBT temperature sensor path
Cracked solder joint on the inverter board
Faulty value transmission to the host controller

P0D78.d: P0D78 is set when the output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor of the electric A/C compressor signals low, which for an NTC sensor means an implausibly hot value. GM uses 274 °C or more in the 2011–2015 Volt and the 2016 ELR, and above 150 °C in the 2016–2019 Volt; detection takes 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms, 40 of 50 at 100 ms or 4 of 5 s, Type B with MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning switched off
c: Short circuit in the IGBT temperature sensor path
Real overheating of the power stage from high load or poor condenser cooling
Faulty value transmission to the host controller

P0D79.d: P0D79 marks an erratic signal from the output driver temperature sensor, the sensor that guards the compressor's power transistors: values flicker or drop out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer publishes set criteria.
s: Air conditioning cuts out repeatedly
Code appears sporadically
c: Cold or cracked solder joint at the IGBT sensor
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the compressor
Switching noise from the inverter coupling into the sensor signal

P0D7A.d: Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase motor whose phase currents U, V and W are measured inside the inverter. P0D7A belongs to phase U.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning does not start
c: Offset or failure of the phase U current sensor in the inverter
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit

P0D7B.d: P0D7B is the second phase U current code of the electric A/C compressor. In GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR it sets when the phase U current sensor reads −68 A or less although the motor is stopped and no speed is requested, counted as 30 failures in 60 samples at 50 ms; Type B, MIL after two trips, with a 12 V reset required before a pass.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning stays off
c: Phase U current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current evaluation

P0D7C.d: P0D7C relates to phase V of the three-phase motor in an electric A/C compressor. GM documents it in the 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 ELR tables as a standstill check: with the compressor speed request at 0 rpm the measured phase V current should be near zero, and a value of +68 A or above in 30 of 60 samples (50 ms each) sets the code.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning inoperative
c: Offset or failure of the phase V current sensor in the inverter
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit

P0D7D.d: P0D7D marks a phase V current reading of the electric A/C compressor that is far negative while the motor should be idle. GM's first-generation Volt and the 2016 ELR set it at −68 A or less, judged in 30 of 60 samples every 50 ms whenever the speed request is zero, as Type B with MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
No cooling from the air conditioning
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
c: Phase V current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current evaluation

P0D7E.d: P0D7E applies to phase W, the third winding of the electric A/C compressor motor. GM's 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR check the W-phase current sensor while the motor is at rest: a reading of +68 A or more in 30 out of 60 samples at 50 ms sets the code, Type B with the MIL after two trips, and only a 12 V reset re-enables a pass.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning does not run
c: Offset or failure of the phase W current sensor channel
Common supply or reference fault in the inverter (several phases affected)

P0D7F.d: P0D7F is the negative-direction current code for phase W of the electric A/C compressor motor. In GM's first-generation Volt and the 2016 ELR the inverter reports a W-phase current of −68 A or lower while the motor is stopped and no speed is requested; 30 such readings in 60 samples at 50 ms set the code, Type B with MIL after two trips, and a 12 V reset is required before it can pass.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning inoperative
c: Phase W current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit

P0D80.d: P0D80 means the on-board charger sees no usable AC supply at its input even though the charging handshake says power should be there. Ford documents the check for its plug-in hybrids in the OBD summaries for model years 2014 to 2018: with the cable connected, the EVSE active and the S2 switch closed, an input below 85 VAC lasting 30 seconds sets the code, and Ford's code dictionary marks it as a MIL code.
s: Vehicle does not charge although the cable is plugged in
Charging fault message or flashing fault pattern at the charge port
Check engine light
c: Charging station or outlet delivers no AC after the handshake (fault, tripped breaker)
Open AC contact or wire between charge inlet and charger
Fault in the charger's input stage or voltage measurement

P0D81.d: P0D81 is the plausibility code for the charger's AC input: a signal is present and electrically valid, yet contradicts the stage the charging sequence has reached. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with thresholds.
s: Charging does not start or stops shortly after plugging in
Charging fault message
c: Charging station switches AC on before the vehicle has closed S2 (faulty or welded EVSE relay)
Charger's input voltage measurement reports an implausible value
Improvised supply that feeds the inlet directly without a proper EVSE

P0D82.d: P0D82 reports that the charger's input circuit signal has dropped below the lowest value the module accepts as electrically valid. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford, for instance, folds missing input into P0D80 with its 85 VAC/30 s limit.
s: Charging does not start
Charging ends earlier than expected
Charging fault message
c: Input sense line or harness shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion at the charge inlet terminals
Failed input stage inside the on-board charger

P0D83.d: P0D83 is set when the charger reads its input circuit above the highest electrically valid level, i.e. a reading the measuring stage could not produce from a healthy mains connection.
s: Charger refuses to charge
Charging fault message
c: Input sense line shorted to a voltage source
Damaged charge inlet with bridged or burnt contacts
Drifted or failed measuring channel in the charger

P0D84.d: P0D84 stands for an input signal that keeps jumping or dropping out during a charge rather than sitting steadily at a wrong value. There is no public manufacturer description of the code.
s: Charging stops and restarts repeatedly
Charging takes noticeably longer
c: Worn, loose or heat-damaged charging plug or inlet contacts
Supply sagging under load, e.g. long extension lead
Loose connector between inlet and charger

P0D85.d: P0D85 means the charger is putting more voltage onto the traction battery side than it should. In Ford's 2019 plug-in hybrid OBD summary the battery controller compares the charger's output voltage with its own request and flags a surplus of 20.82 V lasting 20 seconds.
s: Charging stops
Hybrid system warning and check engine light
c: Voltage control fault inside the on-board charger/DC-DC unit
Open high-voltage fuse or P/N line between charger and battery (output unloaded)
Control unit software error (e.g. Porsche DME, reprogramming)

P0D86.d: Many plug-in vehicles light up the charge inlet to show whether the plug is recognised, charging is running or a fault exists; a Ford summary describes a four-segment ring, a supplier patent multi-coloured LEDs at the port. P0D86 says the control module driving channel A of this indicator finds no continuity in that circuit.
s: Part of the charge port lighting stays dark
Charging status not visible at the inlet, charging itself works
c: Indicator connector at the charge inlet unplugged or not latched
Broken wire in the harness near the charge port flap
Failed LED or lamp element of channel A

P0D87.d: P0D87 flags channel A of the charge port status indicator as pulled low, which in practice means a short to ground somewhere between driver and lamp. Such a fault only shows when the channel is switched on: the driver tries to raise the line and current flows straight to ground.
s: Indicator channel A stays dark when it should light
Charging status hard to read at the port
c: Chafed wire of channel A touching body ground
Water ingress into the charge inlet lighting

P0D88.d: P0D88 is stored when channel A of the charge port status indicator sits at a high level although the driver is holding it off, typically because the line touches a voltage-carrying wire or the driver stage leaks. The fault is therefore seen in the switched-off state; GM's Volt evaluated its own charge-status LED (P0D2C) for short to battery only while the LED was meant to be dark.
s: Indicator channel A lights constantly or glows faintly
Port shows a misleading charging status
c: Channel A wire shorted to a voltage-carrying wire (pinched harness)
Bridged or corroded connector at the indicator
Leaking or failed output stage in the control module

P0D89.d: P0D89 reports lost continuity in the second output channel, B, of the charge port status indicator. Where an indicator has several channels, they usually stand for different colours or segments, as in the multi-colour port lighting of a supplier patent; which one is B depends on the vehicle, and no manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: One colour or segment of the port lighting missing
Charging works normally
c: Break in the channel B wire or its connector pin
Failed LED or segment of channel B
Shared connector or ground at the inlet (when A and C are also affected)

P0D8A.d: P0D8A means channel B of the charge port status indicator is held at ground level when it ought to rise, i.e. a short to ground on the B line or inside its lamp.
s: Colour or segment B stays dark
Charging status only partly shown
c: Wet or corroded contacts at the inlet lighting bridging to ground
Channel B wire chafed through to body ground
Shorted LED or segment of channel B

P0D8B.d: P0D8B is set when the B line of the charge port status indicator carries voltage while its driver has it switched off. The detection logic mirrors what GM published for the Volt's charge-status LED (P0D2C): a short to battery is looked for during the off phase.
s: Colour or segment B stays lit
Displayed charge level does not match the actual state
c: Insulation damage where the harness bends at the flap, contact with a supply wire
Driver output in the control module stuck on

P0D8C.d: P0D8C points to an open third channel, C, of the charge port status indicator. Only systems with at least three separately driven lighting outputs use it, for instance one per colour in an RGB-type port lamp of the kind a supplier patent describes, or individual ring segments.
s: One colour or segment of the port lighting missing
Fault appears after body or inlet repair
