c: Lamp connector left unplugged or pin pushed back after work at the inlet
Failed LED of channel C (on integrated inlets the whole inlet assembly)

P0D8D.d: P0D8D marks channel C of the charge port status indicator as shorted toward ground: when the module switches C on, the line does not reach the expected level and the driver registers overcurrent or a low voltage. As with A and B, the code is defined in the standard but no manufacturer publishes its own conditions for it; GM's Volt logic for P0D2C, which tests a grounded LED line only while the LED is commanded on, sh
s: Colour or segment C stays dark
Whole port indicator may switch off
c: Short to ground at the far end of the harness inside the inlet housing
Shorted LED or segment of channel C
Grounded driver output inside the control module

P0D8E.d: P0D8E is recorded when channel C of the charge port status indicator shows a high level that the driver did not command, a short to a supply voltage or a driver that no longer turns off. Following the pattern GM published for the Volt's charge-status LED, this is checked while the output is meant to be inactive.
s: Colour or segment C lit permanently
Port shows a fault or complete status that is not real
c: Chafed channel C wire touching a supply wire at the flap mechanism
Output stage in the control module stuck on

P0D8F.d: P0D8F means the cooling of on-board charger A is not keeping the unit within its temperature limits, so the charger has to restrict its function. Mercedes documents the code with failure type 97 for the AMG GLE 53 Hybrid (bulletin LI47.70-P-079963, 2025): AC charging stops after about 15 minutes, the cluster reports AC charging inoperative and severely limited hybrid performance, and alongside P0D8F the charger store
s: AC charging stops after a short time or runs at reduced power
Warning that AC charging is inoperative
Hybrid drive performance limited
c: Low coolant level or air in the charger's cooling circuit
Coolant lines connected to the wrong circuit (Mercedes AMG GLE 53 Hybrid)
Failed coolant pump of the low-temperature circuit
Blocked low-temperature radiator or inactive cooling fan

P0D90.d: P0D90 is stored when the AC supplied to the on-board charger does not have a believable mains frequency. No official manufacturer document available to the public names the code with a threshold.
s: Often no noticeable effect apart from the stored code
Charging interrupted at certain supply points
c: Charging from a source with unstable frequency (small generator, inverter)
Faulty portable charging unit or wall box
Fault in the charger's frequency measurement

P0D91.d: P0D91 means the module that drives the charge-plug latch sees its lock output as electrically open: when it commands the latch closed, no current flows through the wiring and actuator winding. Without a confirmed lock, the car normally refuses to start a charging session, because the plug could be withdrawn under load.
s: Vehicle does not charge on AC
Check engine light on (Mercedes)
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
c: Connector at the lock actuator loose, corroded or backed out
Broken wire in the harness between control unit and inlet
Motor winding inside the lock actuator burnt through
Driver stage or software of the controlling module (Mercedes names both)

P0D92.d: P0D92 says the voltage on the lock control output stays too low, typically because the drive line is shorted to ground or the actuator draws far too much current, so the module cannot energise the latch properly and shuts its driver off. No manufacturer publishes this exact code.
s: Charging session does not start after plugging in
Charge plug is not held in the inlet
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
c: Lock drive wire chafed and shorted to body ground
Actuator jammed or binding, drawing excessive current
Water in the actuator connector at the inlet
Driver output of the controlling module defective

P0D93.d: P0D93 reports a lock control circuit that reads higher than the module expects, classically a drive line shorted to a supply voltage. Ford shows that mechanical damage leads there as well: TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 list P0D93:00, alongside P0D94, P0D98, P0D9E and P0DA0, as stored by the SOBDM (secondary on-board diagnostic module) of Mach-E, e-Transit and F-150 Lightning built 2021–2023.
s: DC fast charging (level 3) inoperative
Charger Service Required indicator in the cluster (Ford)
Locking pin visibly broken or absent at the inlet
c: Locking pin broken or missing after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Lock drive wire shorted to a supply voltage
Internal electrical fault in the lock actuator
Driver stage of the controlling module defective

P0D94.d: P0D94 is the functional check of the locking step: the wiring tests fine, yet after a lock command the feedback from the actuator does not confirm that the pin arrived in its locked position. Two makers publish it.
s: Charging aborts or does not start; DC fast charging unavailable
Charge cable cannot be removed except with the manual release
Charge LED changes from green to red, AC charging restricted message (Audi)
c: Software fault in the on-board charger, fixed by update (Audi)
Actuator mechanism binding from dirt, ice or wear
Charge plug not fully seated, so the pin cannot engage

P0D95.d: P0D95 concerns the release direction: the output that withdraws the locking pin shows an open circuit when the module commands unlock. Because J2012 assigns lock and unlock separate control circuits, the module watches each drive direction on its own, and a break can disable only the release.
s: Charge cable stays locked in the inlet after charging
Plug can only be freed with the emergency release
Charging system fault message
c: Open unlock drive wire or loose pin in the actuator connector
Motor winding or internal contact of the actuator open
Corrosion in the connector at the inlet from road splash
Unlock driver stage of the controlling module defective

P0D96.d: P0D96 indicates that the voltage on the unlock control output is too low, which usually means the release line is shorted to ground or the actuator pulls an overcurrent as soon as it is energised in the release direction. To protect its driver, the module stops commanding, so the pin stays where it is.
s: Charge plug cannot be unplugged after charging
Emergency release needed to free the cable
Next charging session refused
c: Unlock drive wire shorted to ground at a chafe point
Actuator seized, for example by ice or dirt, causing overcurrent
Unlock driver stage of the module defective

P0D97.d: P0D97 reports that the unlock control output sits higher than it should while the module is not driving it, or does not follow the command, which points to a release line touching a supply voltage. Such a fault is critical for safety logic: a release path that may be energised unintentionally could free the plug during current flow, so control units typically end the charging session or refuse to begin it while the c
s: Charging session stops or does not start
Plug is not held firmly in the inlet
Charging system fault message
c: Unlock drive wire shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Internal short inside the lock actuator
Unlock driver stage of the module stuck on

P0D98.d: P0D98 is set when the release command is carried out electrically but the feedback does not confirm that the pin has retracted, or the actuator never reaches its open end stop. Ford is the only maker that names it publicly: TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 list P0D98:00 in the SOBDM of Ford's electric Mach-E, e-Transit and Lightning pickup (2021–2023), together with P0D93, P0D94 and the lock position codes P0D9E/P0DA0.
s: DC fast charging (level 3) inoperative
Charger Service Required indicator (Ford)
Plug hard to remove or held in the inlet
c: Actuator pin damaged by pulling the plug while latched (Ford)
Release movement blocked by ice, dirt or a worn gear train

P0D99.d: P0D99 flags a general electrical fault in temperature sensor A of the charging inlet, the element that tells the car how hot the power contacts are. At high current, contact resistance heats the pins; the reading lets the car throttle or stop charging (TE Connectivity, US10960781B2).
s: High-voltage battery cannot be charged
Charging only at reduced power
Charging system fault message
c: Loose low-voltage connector at the on-board charger (smart)
Damaged sensor wiring between inlet and charger
Temperature element in the inlet failed (usually replaced with the inlet harness)
Evaluation input in the charger module defective

P0D9A.d: P0D9A covers a coupler temperature signal that is electrically valid but does not make sense, for example a rise that the charging current cannot explain or a value that disagrees with the rest of the system. GM's preliminary information PIT5904 lists it, with P298C and P0E5F, for the 2022 GMC Hummer EV and BrightDrop EV600: the MIL comes on and charging fails or aborts, often at heavily used public or dealer station
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging fails or stops, often at busy public stations
Code returns only after a drive of about 10 minutes (GM)
c: Oversized or damaged terminals in the charging station plug (GM)
Charging software calibration, update pending or available (GM)
Raised contact resistance at the vehicle inlet pins
Temperature element drifting out of its characteristic

P0D9B.d: P0D9B means the voltage of coupler temperature sensor A has dropped below its valid window. Low refers to the signal, and what that implies about temperature depends on the element: with an NTC a low voltage stands for an extremely hot reading, whereas the PTC chain and Pt 1000 sensors Phoenix Contact builds into its inlets lose resistance as they cool, so in the usual pull-up wiring a low signal looks implausibly co
s: Charging refused or limited
Charging system fault message
Fault stored as intermittent or static in the charger
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the sensor contacts in the inlet
Diagnosis misled by swapped fault texts in the charger (Bentley)

P0D9C.d: P0D9C is stored when the signal of coupler temperature sensor A climbs above its valid window, the typical result of an open sensor loop, an unplugged connector or a short to a supply voltage. Read as temperature, a high signal means cold for an NTC but hot for the resistive PTC and Pt 1000 elements found in CCS inlets from Phoenix Contact, which is why an interrupted Pt 1000 wire can look like a contact far above th
s: Charging stops immediately or does not start
Charging system fault message
Fault stored as intermittent or static in the charger
c: Open sensor wire or connector at the inlet or charger
Sensor signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Temperature element open inside the inlet
Diagnosis misled by swapped fault texts in the charger (Bentley)

P0D9D.d: P0D9D is logged when the signal of temperature sensor A in the charging inlet jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing for good. The sensor sits beside the power pins so the car can cut back or end charging once contact resistance heats them; TE Connectivity patents US10960781B2 and US11117478B2 name thermistors and resistance thermometers for this job.
s: Charging stops now and then and resumes on a later attempt
Charging power reduced for a while without an obvious reason
Charging fault message that comes and goes
c: Sensor wiring between inlet and charger with a loose or chafed contact
Low-voltage connector at the on-board charger not fully seated (seen on smart for sibling codes)
Moisture or corrosion in the inlet harness connector
Temperature element in the inlet with an internal intermittent break

P0D9E.d: The lock position sensor tells the vehicle whether the pin that holds the charging plug in the inlet is extended or retracted. Without that feedback the car cannot confirm a latched plug and refuses fast charging.
s: DC fast charging inoperative
Charger Service Required message in the cluster (Ford)
Locking pin visibly damaged or absent at the inlet
c: Actuator pin broken or missing after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Open or shorted feedback wire between lock actuator and control module
Corroded or loose connector at the lock actuator
Evaluation input of the controlling module defective

P0D9F.d: P0D9F covers a lock position signal that is electrically in range but does not fit the situation: the pin is reported in a position the actuator was not told to reach, or it gets there too late. The sensing principle in GM patent US8936482B2 works on pin travel, so a jammed or worn mechanism shows up here as well as a drifting sensor.
s: Vehicle will not start and reports a connected charging cable (smart)
High-voltage battery does not charge
Fault may appear only at the start or end of charging, with cold or warm parts
c: Loose low-voltage contacts at the 22 kW on-board charger (smart)
Lock mechanism sluggish from ice, dirt or a worn gear train
Position sensor in the actuator drifting or misaligned

P0DA0.d: P0DA0 means the lock position feedback sits at the bottom of its range, typically from a signal wire shorted to ground. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the IGCT supply on, the PHEV-ECU detects a low input from the lock position reading.
s: DC fast charging not possible
Charger Service Required message (Ford)
Plug is not latched or charging ends right after start
c: Lock position signal line shorted to ground (Mitsubishi)
Actuator pin broken after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Position sensor in the inlet harness outside its resistance specification

P0DA1.d: P0DA1 is the high-side fault of the lock position feedback: the signal stays near its upper limit, which points to an open circuit somewhere in the sensor loop rather than a grounded wire. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi sets it in the PHEV-ECU when the supply is on and a high input from the lock position reading is seen.
s: Charging plug lock not confirmed, DC charging refused
Charging system message, no MIL documented
c: Ground connection of the lock actuator connector interrupted
Open signal line between inlet harness and PHEV-ECU
Position sensor in the inlet harness open or far above 16.8 kOhm

P0DA2.d: P0DA2 is stored when the lock position feedback flickers or drops out briefly, while it never sits at one limit long enough for the low or high verdict. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: DC fast charging aborts at random
Lock status message that appears and clears again
c: Loose or corroded contact at the lock actuator connector
Inlet harness chafed where it moves with the charge port flap or body
Worn lock mechanism letting the pin rattle near a switching point

P0DA3.d: The inverter of drive motor B, usually the rear electric motor in all-wheel-drive hybrids, measures its own DC link voltage; sensor A delivers that value to the motor controller. P0DA3 is the general circuit fault for this channel, with no finer verdict such as low or high.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Rear electric drive reduced or unavailable
Reduced power or no READY state
c: Voltage sensing circuit inside the rear motor control unit defective
Loose high-voltage cable or terminal at the rear inverter
Low-voltage connector or harness to the inverter controller faulty

P0DA4.d: P0DA4 flags a rear inverter voltage that is electrically valid but disagrees with the other voltage readings on the same high-voltage bus. Mitsubishi spells out the check for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: once the power drive unit has at least 8 V, voltage control is off, CAN is healthy and the rear value is available, all three comparisons must fail together, namely capacitor 2 main, capacitor 2 sub and capacitor 1 each
s: Plug-in hybrid system warning and MIL on
Rear motor power limited
Code returns only after the OBD-II drive cycle
c: Rear inverter voltage sensing drifts against the other bus readings
Power drive unit faulty (Mitsubishi final repair step)
Underlying fault in the rear motor control unit (P0C7A, P0DA5, P0DA6, P30D1)

P0DA5.d: P0DA5 reports that the rear inverter voltage signal sits at the bottom of its range, the classic result of an open circuit, a short to ground or no high voltage arriving at all. Mitsubishi sets it in the rear motor control unit of the 2018 Outlander PHEV when, with the propulsion system active, the sensor output stays below 0.5 V, roughly 10 V on the bus, for 0.3 s.
s: MIL and plug-in hybrid warning on
Rear motor drive switched off
Possible no-READY condition if other units also lose voltage
c: Rear high-voltage battery cable (P and N lines) loose or damaged
High-voltage fuse not seated or loose bus bar in the battery
Sensing circuit in the rear motor control unit failed
Fault inside the traction battery pack

P0DA6.d: P0DA6 is the upper-limit fault of the rear inverter voltage signal: the reading sticks near the top, as with a short to the sensor supply, or the bus really is overvolted. Mitsubishi checks it in the rear motor control unit of the 2018 Outlander PHEV whenever that unit is powered with 8 to 16 V; a sensor output above 4.7 V, standing for about 440 V, held for 0.3 s sets the code.
s: MIL and plug-in hybrid warning on
Rear motor drive switched off, reduced power
c: Rear motor control unit sensing faulty when no other unit reports high voltage (Mitsubishi)
Fault in the high-voltage circuit or battery when front and generator units also report high
Signal shorted to the sensor supply inside the inverter

P0DA7.d: P0DA7 is meant for a rear inverter voltage reading that jitters or drops out briefly without staying out of range long enough for P0DA5 or P0DA6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hybrid warning that appears and clears
Brief loss of rear drive power
c: Low-voltage connector at the rear inverter with intermittent contact
High-voltage terminal at the rear inverter not tightened properly
Voltage sensing electronics failing with temperature or vibration

P0DA8.d: P0DA8 compares the traction battery voltage with the voltage measured at the inverter of drive motor A; both should match closely once the contactors are closed. Denso cites earlier diagnostics that blame a voltage sensor when the two differ by more than a set amount (US9819293B2).
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Fail-safe electric mode with strongly limited speed (Honda)
Discharged 12 V battery (Ford Mach-E)
c: Cracked solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda Civic/ILX Hybrid)
Battery cell voltage sensor software misreading inverter noise (Honda Accord Hybrid recall)
High-voltage battery junction box faulty (Ford Mach-E)
Battery-side or inverter-side voltage sensor drifting

P0DA9.d: P0DA9 is the motor B counterpart of P0DA8: the controller compares traction battery voltage with the voltage seen at the inverter of drive motor B, typically the rear motor, and logs the code when the two drift apart with the contactors closed. No manufacturer documents P0DA9 publicly.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Rear electric drive limited or disabled
c: Voltage sensing in the motor B inverter drifting
Battery pack voltage measurement in the battery management faulty
High resistance in a contactor, fuse or cable between battery and rear inverter

P0DAA.d: P0DAA reports that the resistance between the charging-side HV bus and chassis ground has fallen too low, so the charging path or the battery is no longer safely insulated. GM documents the logic for the 2014 Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR in the HPC2 (VICM): in charge-only mode the active isolation resistance is measured, at most once per wake-up; below 325 kOhm, or 400 kOhm while the code is active, for 10 s, and
s: Vehicle will not charge
MIL on (GM Type A)
Low coolant level in the battery coolant reservoir
c: Coolant leaking into the battery pack (GM)
Insulation loss within battery cells or sections (GM)
Damaged insulation in the on-board charger or charging cables

P0DAB.d: P0DAB is the overall verdict on cell balancing: the battery controller sees that bleeding charge off the fuller cells no longer brings the pack back into line, so the spread between cells stays too wide. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3) requires hybrids to check exactly this.
s: Check engine light and hybrid system warning in the cluster
Mild hybrid assist, start-stop and regeneration switched off (engine-only operation on Mazda)
Reduced electric range or usable battery capacity
c: Battery controller software that judges balancing too strictly (FCA BPCM and Mazda MSP66 reflash)
Cells aged unevenly so the spread grows faster than balancing can correct it
Internal fault in the battery assembly (Mazda 48 V battery replaced when the code returns at once)
One or more balancing switches or resistors no longer working

P0DAC.d: P0DAC reports an electrical fault in balancing circuit A, meaning the wiring, switch or monitoring chip behind it, not a balancing result. Audi uses it on the e-tron GT (2022-2026) in battery management address 008C and spells it out as an electrical fault of cell controller 1.
s: Battery management warning or red onboard supply lamp
Vehicle may refuse to start or enter drive readiness
Diagnostic tester proposes replacing HV battery modules
c: Brief 12 V supply interruption, e.g. while reconnecting the 12 V battery (Audi e-tron GT)
Defective cell monitoring controller or balancing switch of circuit A
Loose or corroded sense/balancing lead connector at the module

P0DAD.d: P0DAD means balancing circuit A keeps draining its cells although the controller has not asked for it: the bleed switch is stuck closed and the resistor keeps pulling those cells down. Ford uses the code in the BECM of its hybrids; the 2019 OBD summary gives each of 14 circuits six cells and, at key-on with the contactors still open, rates a circuit faulty when one of its cells departs from the mean for 0.1 s by over
s: Hybrid or EV battery warning with the MIL
Cells of one group noticeably lower after the car has been parked
Range or electric assistance decreasing over days
c: Balancing transistor of circuit A shorted (fails closed)
Monitoring chip or its drive output keeps the switch enabled
Controller software leaving a balancing request active

P0DAE.d: With P0DAE the controller has commanded balancing on circuit A, yet nothing happens: the switch stays open or the bleed resistor is broken, so the targeted cells keep their charge. Ford documents the code for its hybrid BECM; in the 2014 OBD summary the verdict rests on a 100 ms check at power-up with open contactors, in which one cell of the six-cell group lying beyond 75 mV from the average on two successive starts
s: MIL and battery system warning
Charging ends early because individual cells reach full first
Growing cell voltage spread in the live data
c: Bleed resistor of circuit A open or its solder joint cracked
Broken balancing/sense lead or terminal between module and cells

P0DAF.d: P0DAF is a plausibility code: circuit A switches and is electrically intact, but the effect on the cell voltages does not match what the controller expects. FCA is the visible user.
s: MIL on, often together with other battery codes
Vehicle may not start or cannot be switched off (Jeep Cherokee hybrid)
Reduced mild hybrid assistance
c: Battery pack control module software with an oversensitive check (FCA bulletins 08-030-24, 08-186-26)
Weak or deeply discharged cells that respond differently to balancing, e.g. after cold cranking
Bleed resistor or switch of circuit A with changed resistance

P0DB0.d: P0DB0 flags an electrical defect in the second balancing circuit, B. The battery controller finds an open, short or implausible voltage on the switch, resistor or lead serving that cell group, independent of whether balancing would be needed right now.
s: Battery system warning and MIL
Electric drive or assistance possibly limited
c: Damaged balancing/sense lead or connector of cell group B
Cell monitoring chip or controller of group B defective
Short 12 V supply dropout during service work

P0DB1.d: P0DB1: in circuit B the bleed path stays closed even after the controller withdrew the command. The cells of group B are drained without pause, so their voltage falls behind the others, worst during long standstill.
s: MIL with battery warning
Group B cells clearly low after parking
Usable charge and range shrinking
c: Shorted balancing transistor in circuit B
Drive output of the monitoring chip stuck active
Moisture or contamination on the module board creating a leakage path

P0DB2.d: Stuck off on circuit B (P0DB2) is the passive failure: the command arrives, but the bleed resistor of that group carries no current, so its high cells are never trimmed. LG Chem's patent EP2730933A1 tests for this by switching the balancing circuit on and off and watching how the voltage across a diagnosis resistor reacts; no change means a dead circuit.
s: MIL and battery warning
Charging stops before the expected state of charge
High cell voltages in group B in live data
c: Bleed resistor of group B burnt open
Balancing transistor of circuit B no longer switching
Open terminal or cell tap connection in group B

P0DB3.d: P0DB3 concerns how well circuit B works rather than whether it switches. The controller balances group B for a set time and then checks the outcome; if the cells moved too little, too much or in an unexpected direction, the result is called implausible.
s: MIL, sometimes without any noticeable drivability change
Cell spread in group B not shrinking after charging
c: Controller software with too narrow expectations (cf. FCA updates for P0DAF)
Aged or high-resistance cell in group B reacting atypically
Bleed resistor value drifted so balancing current is wrong

P0DB4.d: P0DB4 belongs to the third balancing channel, C, and points to its hardware: an interrupted or shorted lead, a failed switch or a monitoring chip reporting nonsense for that cell group. A common test method sits in LG Chem's EP2730933A1, where a diagnosis resistor between cell and balancing circuit lets the controller see a defined voltage step each time the circuit is toggled; a missing or wrong step betrays the fau
s: MIL with battery or hybrid warning
Further cell voltage codes stored alongside
Electric operation possibly reduced
c: Fault in a lead shared by voltage sensing and balancing in group C
Cell monitoring chip of group C defective
Corroded module connector after water ingress

P0DB5.d: Circuit C stuck on (P0DB5) means the cells of group C bleed energy permanently, also with the car switched off. Designers guard against exactly this: the LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 lets every balance enable expire on a timer unless the central controller renews it, so a lost command cannot leave a switch on.
s: MIL with battery warning, often after standing
Low cell voltage codes in group C as a follow-up
Electric range dropping
c: Balancing transistor in circuit C failed closed
Enable or watchdog logic of the module not releasing the switch
Leakage path on the module board

P0DB6.d: P0DB6 says that the bleed function of group C does not respond: commanded on, circuit C stays dead. In LG Chem's US20110285539A1 such a case shows up because a test capacitor charged to cell voltage is not emptied through the balancing path and keeps a high residual voltage.
s: MIL with battery warning
Shorter charging sessions and lower usable capacity
c: Bleed resistor of circuit C open
Balancing transistor of circuit C not conducting
Broken cell tap or weld in group C

P0DB7.d: P0DB7 covers a circuit C that works electrically but whose outcome does not add up. A typical trigger is a cell in group C that needs trimming far more often or far less often than its neighbours.
s: MIL, often with no other immediate effect
One cell in group C repeatedly lower than the rest
c: Cell in group C with rising self-discharge or an internal short
Controller software with unsuitable plausibility limits
Bleed resistor of circuit C out of tolerance

P0DB8.d: P0DB8 is the circuit code for balancing channel D. Here the controller sees a hardware problem: the switch, resistor or cell tap of group D reports a state that cannot be valid, typically an open lead or a short to a neighbouring line.
s: MIL and battery system message
Possible limitation of electric power
c: Open balancing terminal or lead in group D
Monitoring chip of group D defective

P0DB9.d: A stuck-on circuit D (P0DB9) drains group D continuously. The usual check is simple: does the switch state reported back equal the state the controller asked for? GM applies this on the eAssist battery for a related code, sampling every 200 ms and logging a Type B fault after 7 mismatches in 10.
s: MIL with battery warning
Group D cells and their local temperature deviating
Loss of charge while parked
c: Balancing transistor of circuit D shorted
Status feedback of the module wrong, switch actually fine
Drive output of the monitoring chip stuck on

P0DBA.d: P0DBA: circuit D refuses to bleed. Toshiba's patent US20130026994A1 lists an open balancing terminal as one of the faults a monitoring chip should report, and this is the typical root of a stuck-off result.
s: MIL and battery warning
Range slowly decreasing, charging finishing early
c: Open balancing terminal or cell tap in group D
Bleed resistor of circuit D open
Balancing transistor of circuit D failed open

P0DBB.d: For P0DBB the controller judges the effect of balancing in circuit D as implausible. A clear reference is GM's eAssist key-off test for a related code: engaging the bleed load has to pull the cell at least 0.1 V away from its rest value.
s: MIL without obvious driving symptoms
Cell spread in group D persisting after long charging
c: Cell in group D with changed internal resistance or capacity
Plausibility limits in the controller software too tight
Bleed resistor of circuit D drifted

P0DBC.d: P0DBC is set for an electrical fault in the fifth balancing channel, E: the controller cannot trust the path through which group E would be bled, because a lead, switch or resistor reads open, shorted or out of range. The floating-capacitor method in LG Chem's US20110285539A1 is one way to test that path without loading the cells: charge, discharge through the balancing circuit, then compare the residual voltage with
s: MIL and battery warning
Electric drive possibly restricted
c: Open or shorted balancing lead in group E
Monitoring chip responsible for group E faulty
Module connector of group E loose or corroded

P0DBD.d: With P0DBD the controller finds circuit E active when it should be idle. LG Chem's EP2730933A1 offers a way to see it: with the balancing circuit commanded off, the voltage across the diagnosis resistor should match the idle pattern; if it looks like the active pattern, current is still flowing.
s: MIL with battery warning
Power reduced as group E cells drop
Charge loss after a few days parked
c: Balancing transistor of circuit E shorted
Drive line of the switch held active by the monitoring chip
Leakage on the module board after moisture

P0DBE.d: P0DBE means circuit E does nothing when told to bleed. The LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 describes reading the cells while a planned bleed phase is running and treating a balancing side that shows no effect as faulted; this is the logic behind a stuck-off verdict.
s: MIL and battery warning
Apparent loss of capacity over weeks
c: Bleed resistor of circuit E open
Balancing transistor of circuit E does not turn on
Enable signal for group E not reaching the module

P0DBF.d: P0DBF tells that balancing in circuit E produces results the controller cannot explain, though the circuit switches. One reason can be a cell that keeps needing correction: the Southwest Electronic Energy patent US9097774B2 tracks how often each cell gets balanced and treats an outlier as a warning of internal shorting, well before overheating.
s: MIL, usually without immediate drivability change
Recurring deviation of a single cell in group E
c: Cell in group E with increased self-discharge
Software limits for the balancing check too narrow
Bleed resistor of circuit E out of tolerance

P0DC0.d: P0DC0 marks an electrical fault in balancing circuit F, the sixth cell group whose bleed path the battery controller can switch. Audi lists P0DC000 for the 2016 A3 e-tron in bulletin 93 17 04 (2046556/1), together with the circuit codes for groups A to H and B200000.
s: Charging fails intermittently
Cluster shows a connected charger although no cable is plugged in
Several balancing circuit codes stored at the same time
c: Battery controller software that starts CAN communication too late (Audi A3 e-tron, J840/JX1 update)
Open or chafed balancing/sense lead of cell group F
Defective cell monitoring chip serving group F

P0DC1.d: P0DC1 says that the bleed path of cell group F appears to stay engaged. Ford lists it for the BECM of its full and plug-in hybrids in the OBD system summaries of model years 2014 to 2019.
s: Check engine light with hybrid battery warning after a cold start
Cells of group F clearly below the pack average after standstill
Reduced electric range or assistance
c: Bleed transistor of group F shorted, so the resistor stays connected
Monitoring chip output keeps the switch of circuit F enabled
A cell of group F with high self-discharge mimicking a drained group

P0DC2.d: With P0DC2 the controller concludes that circuit F does not bleed when asked to, so the fullest cells of group F are never trimmed. Ford's 2014 hybrid OBD summary applies the same 75 mV deviation test over the six cells of each circuit as for the stuck-on code, but the 2014 to 2018 versions want the deviation seen at two power-ups in a row, before the contactors close.
s: Charging ends earlier than usual, displayed full charge gives less range
Cells of group F remain highest after charging
Check engine light, usually without noticeable driving change
c: Bleed resistor of group F burnt open
Bleed transistor of circuit F no longer conducting
Loose cell tap or connector pin on the balancing lead

P0DC3.d: P0DC3 is the plausibility code for balancing circuit F, and Volvo is a documented user. On the SPA Twin Engine plug-in hybrids (XC90, XC60, S90, V90, model years 2016-2019) the BECM stores P0DC300 as an intermittent fault, listed alongside the range/performance codes of circuits A to E.
s: Displayed electric range fluctuates or is unreasonably low
Combustion engine runs more often than expected in hybrid mode
Check engine light, fault often stored as intermittent
c: BECM software version with faulty balancing evaluation (Volvo TJ 33931)
Cells of group F with changed capacity respond differently to bleeding
Bleed resistor value drifted so the balancing current is off target

P0DC4.d: P0DC4 points to the hardware path of balancing circuit G: lead, switch, resistor or the chip that drives them. On the 2016 Audi A3 e-tron it appears as P0DC400 in bulletin 93 17 04, never alone but in a row with the circuit codes of groups A to H.
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
External charging refused now and then
Scan tool lists several circuit codes plus a control module fault
c: Common software or communication cause when circuit codes A to H appear together (Audi A3 e-tron)
Bleed FET of channel G failing the on-state check
Corroded or loose connector on the cell harness of group G

P0DC5.d: P0DC5 reports that the bleed switch of group G seems to stay closed. Ford lists the code for the BECM of its 2018 hybrids and plug-ins; there, a sticking circuit is inferred at start-up, with contactors open, from any of its six cells straying more than 75 mV from the pack average.
s: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning
Low cell voltage codes may follow after longer parking
Electric range decreasing from day to day
c: Balancing switch of group G stuck in conduction
Enable signal from the controller or chip never withdrawn
Moisture or contamination forming a leakage path on the module board

P0DC6.d: P0DC6 is set when circuit G stays idle although balancing is requested, so group G cannot give up charge. Ford names the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary and decides it from the start-up voltage comparison of the six cells per circuit.
s: Electric range shrinks gradually over weeks
Charging stops before the indicated target
Check engine light without immediate drivability change
c: Shunt resistor of group G open, no current can bypass the cells
Balancing switch of group G does not close on command
Pin backed out of the cell harness connector

P0DC7.d: P0DC7 means circuit G switches but its effect on the cells does not fit the controller's model. The code is not tied to passive bleeding.
s: Check engine light with hybrid system message
Cell spread in group G does not shrink after balancing
Usable battery capacity slightly reduced
c: Controller software with too tight plausibility limits
Weak transfer stage in active balancing (capacitor or transformer aged)
Cells of group G aged so that they react differently to correction

P0DC8.d: P0DC8 covers an electrical fault of balancing circuit H. Audi's bulletin 93 17 04 for the 2016 A3 e-tron lists P0DC800 as the last of its circuit codes; no letter beyond H appears there, which suggests eight circuits in that pack.
s: Charging not possible at times
Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
Fault returns after clearing until software is updated
c: Cell electronics not answering in time after wake-up (Audi software fix)
Damaged internal bus or supply wiring to the monitoring board of group H
Open bleed path or lead in circuit H

P0DC9.d: P0DC9: the bleed path of group H keeps conducting. Ford lists the code for its 2016 hybrid and plug-in BECM, judged at start-up from the cell spread within the six-cell circuit.
s: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning
Group H noticeably lower than the rest after parking
Locally raised temperature reading in the battery module
c: Bleed FET of group H shorted and unaffected by thermal pause
Heat damage on the monitoring board around the bleed resistors of H
Chip logic keeping the balancing enable of channel H active

P0DCA.d: P0DCA flags circuit H as inactive: balancing was ordered, but group H keeps its charge. Ford includes the code in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary, again decided by the start-up comparison of six cells per circuit with the pack average.
s: Full charge reached earlier, with less range than before
Cells of group H stay at the top of the cell list
Check engine light
c: Bleed resistor of group H open
Broken cell tap or weld on the balancing lead of H
Intended stop (timer, thermal pause) wrongly judged as no response by the software

P0DCB.d: P0DCB is raised when circuit H works electrically but the result of a balancing run does not match the plan. Ford's patent US9145064B2 shows how such a plan can be made: from each cell's capacity surplus and the pack charge current the controller computes how long that cell's resistor must stay active during charging so that all cells reach the target together.
s: Check engine light, often only after charging sessions
Group H remains out of line after a full charge
Fluctuating range estimate
c: Wrong capacity or state-of-charge estimate for the cells of group H
Battery controller software (update first, as Volvo does for P0DC3)
Bleed resistor of H drifted from its nominal value

P0DCC.d: P0DCC concerns the hardware of balancing circuit I, the ninth group, so only packs split into at least nine balancing channels can raise it. No maker publishes this exact code: Ford's hybrid summaries assign letter I only to the stuck codes P0DCD and P0DCE, and Audi's A3 e-tron bulletin stops at H.
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Electric drive or charging limited by the battery controller
c: Broken balancing or sense lead of group I
Corroded connector between cell group I and its monitoring board
Defective monitoring chip for channel I

P0DCD.d: P0DCD tells that circuit I is drained although no balancing is wanted. In Ford's 2014 hybrid OBD summary the code belongs to the start-up check with open contactors; that early version only sets it after the 75 mV spread within the six-cell group has shown up on two consecutive power-ups.
s: Check engine light with hybrid battery warning at start-up
Group I lower than the rest after longer standstill
Shorter electric range
c: Balancing switch of group I permanently conducting
Software leaving a deliberate switch activation (e.g. chip warming) active
Driver stage of the monitoring chip stuck active on channel I

P0DCE.d: P0DCE means the bleed path of group I does not respond to a balancing request. Ford lists it in the 2019 OBD summary for its full and plug-in hybrids, where the BECM discharges only the highest cells to match the rest and runs this check for 100 ms at power-up before the contactors close.
s: Electric range decreases over many charging cycles
Cells of group I highest at the end of charging
Check engine light without noticeable effect while driving
c: Open bleed resistor in circuit I
Balancing switch of group I that no longer closes
Cell tap of group I loose at the busbar

P0DCF.d: P0DCF closes the series for the ninth balancing group: circuit I is electrically intact, yet balancing does not bring its cells to where the controller intended. No maker publishes this code.
s: Check engine light, typically noticed after charging
Group I stays apart from the other cells after a full charge
Slowly shrinking electric range
c: Cells of group I aged differently, so the planned balancing time no longer fits
Battery controller calibration with an unsuitable target or time window
Bleed resistor of circuit I off its nominal value, giving too little current

P0DD0.d: P0DD0 reports an electrical fault in balancing circuit J, the tenth group. Only packs split into ten or more balancing channels can set it; Audi's A3 e-tron bulletin ends its circuit codes at H and Volvo's SPA Twin Engine journal at F, so those packs never reach J.
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Charging or electric drive limited by the battery controller
c: Open balancing or sense terminal of group J (lead, crimp or weld)
Loose or corroded connector between group J and its monitoring board
Faulty monitoring chip channel serving circuit J

P0DD1.d: P0DD1: group J's bleed path keeps drawing current after balancing should have ended. Ford's 2014 OBD summary for its hybrids and plug-ins assigns the code to the BECM, which checks at power-up, before the contactors close, for 100 ms: if one of the six cells in the circuit sits more than 75 mV away from the mean of all cells, and this repeats on two consecutive power cycles, the fault is stored.
s: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning after switching on
Group J clearly lower than the rest after parking
Shorter electric range
c: Balancing transistor of group J shorted and conducting permanently
Balancing enable for channel J not withdrawn by the monitoring electronics
Cell in group J with high self-discharge producing the same voltage pattern

P0DD2.d: P0DD2 marks circuit J as unable to bleed: balancing is commanded, but the six cells of group J keep their charge. Ford lists the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary with the same power-up test as for the stuck-on case, run for 100 ms with the contactors still open, two consecutive power cycles and the 75 mV limit against the average cell voltage.
s: Check engine light without noticeable change in driving
Cells of group J at the top of the cell list at the end of charging
Usable battery capacity declining over time
c: Bleed resistor of circuit J open or burnt
Balancing switch of group J no longer closing
Interrupted balancing lead between cell tap and board

P0DD3.d: P0DD3 is a plausibility verdict on circuit J: the switch reacts, but the effect of balancing on group J does not match what the controller expected. No maker documents this code publicly, so the reasoning rests on CARB and on how balancing is planned.
s: Check engine light, often only after several charges
Group J remains out of line despite balancing
Unsteady range prediction
c: Wrong charge estimate for the cells of group J
Battery controller software or calibration (check for updates first)
Balancing path of J with raised resistance, so less charge moves than planned

P0DD4.d: P0DD4 is the electrical fault code for balancing circuit K, the eleventh group, so it only exists on packs with at least eleven balancing channels. Public maker documents for this exact code were not found; Ford's summaries give K only to the stuck faults P0DD5 and P0DD6.
s: Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Missing or implausible cell voltages for group K in the scan tool
Reduced charging or drive power
c: Open wire or loose cell tap in group K
Corrosion or moisture at the connector of the monitoring board for K
Defective monitoring chip or external balancing part of channel K

P0DD5.d: P0DD5 tells that circuit K is discharging its cells without a balancing request. Ford's 2016 hybrid OBD summary links the code to the BECM start-up check: before the contactors close it looks at the six cells of the circuit for 100 ms and fails it when one of them is more than 75 mV away from the average, confirmed on a second power cycle.
s: Check engine light at start-up
Group K drops faster than the other cells while parked
Locally higher battery module temperature
c: Shorted balancing switch of group K
Heat damage or contamination bridging the balancing path of K on the board
Driver stage of the monitoring chip holding channel K on

P0DD6.d: P0DD6: group K's bleed path stays dead when balancing is called for. Ford includes it in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary; the BECM decides at power-up with open contactors, within 100 ms and over two power cycles, using the 75 mV deviation of one of the six cells from the average.
s: Check engine light while the car drives normally
Group K highest at the end of charging
Electric range decreasing over many charges
c: Open bleed resistor in circuit K
Balancing switch of group K failing to turn on
Cracked solder joint in the balancing path of K

P0DD7.d: P0DD7 points to balancing of group K that works, but not within the expected limits. No maker publishes this code.
s: Check engine light, often after charging
Spread of group K returns soon after a balancing session
Fluctuating range estimate
c: Balancing current of K below the expected value (aged resistor, raised contact resistance)
Controller calibration with too short balancing time for group K
A cell in group K drifting faster than balancing can compensate

P0DD8.d: P0DD8 concerns the hardware of balancing circuit L, the twelfth group. No manufacturer documents it publicly; Ford, whose hybrid BECM runs through letter N, uses L only in the stuck codes P0DD9 and P0DDA.
s: Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
Power or charging limited
c: Open resistor, switch or solder joint in circuit L
Poor connection of the cell taps of group L
Faulty voltage measuring channel next to circuit L

P0DD9.d: P0DD9: the balancing path of group L will not switch off. The 2018 edition of Ford's hybrid OBD summary contains the code; the BECM catches it at power-up with the contactors still open, in a 100 ms check that compares each of the six cells of circuit L with the average and fails above 75 mV, again over two power cycles.
s: Check engine light after switching on
Group L lower than the others after standing
Less electric range
c: Balancing switch of group L shorted
Switch status feedback of channel L reporting on although the switch is open
Balancing command for L not cleared by the monitoring electronics

P0DDA.d: P0DDA says circuit L does not discharge when it is told to. In Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary the start-up test has been simplified: it still runs for 100 ms before the contactors close, but the requirement of two consecutive power cycles is gone, and the 75 mV deviation of a cell from the average must instead persist for 0.1 s.
s: Check engine light with no change in drivability
Group L reaches full charge before the rest
Gradual loss of usable capacity
c: Balancing switch of group L stays open when commanded on
Bleed resistor of circuit L open
Missing gate drive for the balancing switch of L

P0DDB.d: P0DDB stands for balancing of group L whose result is out of range although the circuit answers. No maker documents P0DDB publicly.
s: Check engine light, sometimes only after long parking
Group L drifting low between charges
Range estimate varying from day to day
c: Cell in group L with an internal soft short, needing balancing again and again
Controller calibration of expected balancing effect for L
Drifted bleed resistor of circuit L

P0DDC.d: P0DDC reports an electrical fault of balancing circuit M, the thirteenth group, which only large packs with at least thirteen channels possess. No maker publishes this exact code; in Ford's BECM documents M appears only as stuck on (P0DDD) and stuck off (P0DDE).
s: Check engine light and hybrid warning
Battery controller restricting power or charging
c: Broken sense or balancing wire of group M
Damaged or poorly seated connector at the board for M
Fault in the monitoring electronics of channel M

P0DDD.d: P0DDD reports a balancing path of group M that keeps conducting. Ford's 2015 hybrid OBD summary places it in the BECM monitor, judged at power-up before the contactors close: 100 ms, six cells per circuit, more than 75 mV from the average, two consecutive power cycles.
s: Check engine light at start-up
Group M noticeably low after overnight parking
Raised module temperature near group M
c: Shorted balancing switch of group M that no timer can stop
Damaged external balancing transistor on the board for M
High self-discharge cell in group M imitating a stuck switch

P0DDE.d: P0DDE means group M is not bled when it should be. Ford carries the code in its 2016 hybrid OBD summary with the usual BECM start-up rule: 100 ms with open contactors, six cells per circuit, a 75 mV gap to the average, confirmed over two power cycles.
s: Check engine light while driving feels normal
Group M highest at the end of each charge
Less usable battery energy over time
c: Bleed resistor of circuit M open
Balancing switch of group M that no longer turns on
Intended balancing stop for M misjudged as no response by the software

P0DDF.d: P0DDF covers group M when balancing responds but its outcome is not credible. No manufacturer publishes this code.
s: Check engine light following charging sessions
Group M not aligned with the rest after full charge
Inconsistent range display
c: Stored capacity value for cells of group M out of date

P0DE0.d: P0DE0 flags a wiring or driver fault in balancing circuit N, the fourteenth and last letter of the series; the next code, P0DE4, belongs to a different system. Packs with more balancing groups than fourteen must therefore map several groups to one letter or use their own codes.
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Electric operation or charging restricted
c: Open balancing terminal or lead of group N
Corroded or loose connector at the last module board
Monitoring chip channel for N defective

P0DE1.d: P0DE1 is the last stuck-on code of the series: group N keeps bleeding when it should rest. Ford lists it in every hybrid OBD summary from 2014 to 2019; in the 2017 edition the BECM spends 100 ms after key-on, while the contactors are still open, checking whether any of the six cells of circuit N sits more than 75 mV from the average, with two consecutive power cycles needed.
s: Check engine light after switching on
Group N drops while the car is parked
Shorter electric range
c: Balancing switch of group N permanently conducting
Cell of group N with an internal short causing the same voltage drop
Monitoring electronics keeping the balancing command for N active

P0DE2.d: P0DE2 closes Ford's list of balancing codes: circuit N does not discharge when commanded. Ford's 2018 hybrid summary has the BECM judge this during a 100 ms window at key-on, contactors still open, comparing each of the six cells with the average against 75 mV over two power cycles.
s: Check engine light without driving complaint
Charging ends early because group N is full first
Electric range shrinking over months
c: Open bleed resistor in circuit N
Balancing switch of group N not turning on
Cell tap of group N detached from the busbar

P0DE3.d: P0DE3 is the final code of the balancing series and judges whether balancing of group N achieves a believable result. No maker documents it publicly.
s: Check engine light, mostly after charging
Group N never quite levels with the other groups
Reduced and unsteady range
c: Cells of group N aged unevenly
Controller estimates or calibration for group N off
Bleed path of N with too little current

P0DE4.d: P0DE4 reports that the electric motor of auxiliary transmission fluid pump A has run too hot. Such a pump keeps the transmission pressurised while the engine is stopped, either by start-stop or during electric driving in a hybrid.
s: Start-stop no longer shuts the engine off
Electric driving limited, engine keeps running
Harsh engagement when pulling away after a stop
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Low, aged or wrong transmission fluid making the pump work harder
Binding rotor or worn bearing in the pump motor
Transmission running hot (towing, heat, restricted fluid cooler)
Faulty temperature evaluation in the pump controller or outdated software

P0DE5.d: P0DE5 flags an interrupted drive circuit for charge status indicator B, a second lamp or LED that tells the owner whether the vehicle is charging, for instance one at the charge port next to the one on the dashboard. Which light gets the letter B is up to the maker.
s: Charge status indicator B stays dark while charging
Charging works normally
Warning lamp possible depending on the manufacturer
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector to indicator B
Burnt-out LED or failed indicator unit
Corroded contacts in the weather-exposed charge port area
Failed output driver in the controlling module

P0DE6.d: P0DE6 means the battery controller has measured at least one cell of the high-voltage pack below its lower voltage limit. It concerns a real reading, not the sensing lines (P0B3D and similar), and it looks at the weakest cell rather than the charge of the whole pack (P0A7D).
s: Vehicle will not start or switch to ready
Reduced power, no electric driving
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Pack deeply discharged after long standing or repeated failed starts
Battery controller software judging too strictly (e.g. cold cranking)
Single weak cell with high self-discharge or lost capacity
Cell balancing circuit draining one cell

P0DE7.d: P0DE7 is stored when a single cell of the high-voltage pack climbs above the upper voltage limit the battery controller permits. Overcharged lithium-ion cells age quickly and can become unsafe, so the controller usually restricts charging and regenerative braking until the cell is back in range.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Weaker regenerative braking, charging limited
Mild-hybrid assist or start-stop unavailable
c: Battery controller software or calibration (documented by Ram)
Cell balancing no longer bleeding off the highest cell
Aged cell with raised internal resistance overshooting during regen
Drifting cell monitoring chip reporting too high a value

P0DE8.d: P0DE8 reports an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit for coolant control valve C, a third switchable valve in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. What it switches depends on the layout, for example whether coolant passes through the radiator, the air-conditioning chiller or a heater, and the maker decides which valve is called C.
s: Battery temperature control works only in a fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced when the pack is too hot or cold
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Broken wire or loose connector at valve C
Open coil or motor winding inside valve C
Corroded pins from coolant or water ingress
Failed driver stage in the controlling module

P0DE9.d: P0DE9 says coolant control valve C is electrically fine but does not do its job: it fails to reach the commanded position or remains in its off state. No manufacturer documents P0DE9 publicly.
s: Battery heats up faster under load or while fast charging
Charging power or drive power limited
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Valve body seized or sluggish from deposits
Worn actuator motor or gearing in valve C
Low coolant or air in the battery loop distorting the temperature check

P0DEA.d: P0DEA means coolant control valve C stays in its active position even though the controller has asked it to return. A wiring check cannot see this, because the circuit is intact; the controller needs a position feedback, as on GM's Volt valve with its own sensor codes, or it infers the state from coolant and pack temperatures that keep moving the wrong way.
s: Pack too cold in winter or too warm in summer
Reduced range or charging speed
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Valve jammed in the active position by debris or wear
Driver stage that does not switch off

P0DEB.d: P0DEB is set when the drive line of coolant control valve C reads too low, which almost always means a short to ground somewhere between controller and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DEB publicly.
s: Valve C no longer moves, temperature control in fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced at temperature extremes
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Chafed wire shorting to body ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve motor

P0DEC.d: P0DEC is the short-to-voltage case for coolant control valve C: its drive line reads high at a moment when the controller expects it low. No manufacturer documents P0DEC publicly.
s: Valve C runs to an end position and stays there
Pack temperature drifts, power or charging limited
Malfunction indicator lamp on
c: Wire pinched against a supply line
Driver stage in the module not switching off
Moisture bridging pins in the connector

P0DED.d: P0DED points to an open or faulty hard-wired circuit between the powertrain side and the pedestrian alert control module, the unit that makes a quiet hybrid or EV audible at low speed. It is not a network fault, which is U013F, nor a speaker fault, which uses B0122 and B0123.
s: No artificial driving sound at low speed or in reverse
Pedestrian alert warning message in the instrument cluster
c: Broken wire or loose connector at the alert module
Blown fuse or interrupted supply to the module
Internal fault of the pedestrian alert module

P0DEE.d: P0DEE is set when the hard-wired circuit to the pedestrian alert control module sits below its expected voltage, typically from a short to ground. No manufacturer documents P0DEE publicly, so the exact signal behind it, whether supply, wake-up or a command line, is not known in detail.
s: Pedestrian warning sound missing
Warning message in the instrument cluster
Fuse for the alert module may be blown
c: Chafed or crushed wire shorting to ground
Water ingress in a connector near bumper or wheel arch
Internal short in the alert module

P0DEF.d: P0DEF reports a voltage above the permitted window on the wired link to the pedestrian alert control module, most often because a wire touches a supply line or the line has lost its ground reference. No manufacturer documents P0DEF publicly.
s: Pedestrian sound missing or sounding at the wrong time
Warning message in the instrument cluster
Possible 12 V battery drain while parked
c: Wire pinched against a 12 V supply line
Loose or corroded ground connection of the module
Internal fault of the alert module or its driver

P0DF0.d: P0DF0 is the catch-all circuit code for temperature sensor B in the generator inverter, the power stage that drives the generator of a two-machine hybrid. The controller sets it when the sensor line is electrically faulty but the fault is not sorted into low, high or erratic.
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output, weaker charging while driving
Hybrid system may switch to a restricted mode
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the inverter or power unit
Thermistor or its signal path inside the inverter module faulty
Faulty evaluation input in the generator control unit

P0DF1.d: P0DF1 means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor B drops out or jumps for short moments and then looks normal again. Typical triggers are temperature steps faster than the power module could physically heat or cool, or brief readings that resemble an open line.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Occasional short loss of generator power
Fault often not reproducible at the workshop
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the inverter connector
Harness chafing or vibration damage near the power unit
Intermittent contact inside the inverter module

P0DF2.d: P0DF2 covers an electrical fault on temperature sensor C of the generator inverter that the controller cannot assign to a more specific low, high or intermittent code. Which power switch carries sensor C is up to the manufacturer; in Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV the third high-side IGBT sensor sits on the W phase, and its faults are logged only as P0DF7 to P0DF9.
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Generator power reduced as a precaution
Higher engine use or weaker battery recharge
c: Thermistor inside the IGBT module defective
Connector or signal line fault between module and controller
Faulty input stage in the generator control unit

P0DF3.d: P0DF3 is logged when sensor C in the generator inverter delivers an unsteady signal: short spikes, gaps or values that change faster than the module temperature ever could. Such faults often start at connectors that loosen under engine vibration and repeated heating cycles, or at pins attacked by moisture.
s: Warning light that appears only now and then
Brief drops in generator power
Code stored as history fault without current symptoms
c: Terminal losing contact under vibration or heat cycles
Moisture or corrosion in the inverter connector
Intermittent connection inside the inverter module

P0DF4.d: P0DF4 reports that temperature sensor B of the generator inverter delivers an electrically valid signal whose value does not fit the other sensors. Mitsubishi documents the check for the Outlander PHEV: a single time in each drive cycle, following at least 600 s of standstill and with the IGBTs switched off, the V-phase high-side sensor may not differ by more than 47 °C from the other two phase sensors for 0.1 s; oth
s: Message such as Propulsion System Service Required
Engine warning light on
Turtle symbol and reduced power in some cases
c: Control software misdetection (Volvo T8, ECM update available)
Sensor in the power module drifted or stuck at one value
Internal fault in the power drive unit (Mitsubishi replaces the unit)

P0DF5.d: P0DF5 sets when the signal voltage of generator inverter temperature sensor B stays below its valid window. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV checks this continuously: if the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor reads at most 1.25 V during 0.08 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply, P0DF5-00 is stored.
s: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Generator output limited, engine runs more often
Displayed inverter temperature implausibly high
c: Shorted thermistor inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit

P0DF6.d: P0DF6 is the high-signal case for sensor B in the generator inverter. In the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi stores P0DF6-00 when the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor voltage reaches at least 3.75 V during 0.08 s, again only with a GCU supply of at least 8 V.
s: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature shown far too low
Generator power reduced
c: Open signal line or backed-out terminal
Cracked sensor element or internal fault of the power drive unit

P0DF7.d: P0DF7 is the plausibility code for temperature sensor C of the generator inverter. The idea behind it: after a long rest every power switch should be at roughly the same temperature, so a sensor that stands out is suspect.
s: Engine warning light on after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Possibly reduced generator power
c: Sensor C drifted or stuck inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit

P0DF8.d: P0DF8 tells that temperature sensor C in the generator inverter delivers a voltage below its valid range. Mitsubishi uses the code in the Outlander PHEV for the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor: a reading at or under 1.25 V for 0.08 s, with at least 8 V GCU supply, stores P0DF8-00, and the check runs all the time.
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Generator power limited
Implausibly high inverter temperature in live data
c: Signal line of sensor C shorted to ground
Coolant or moisture inside the inverter electronics
Shorted sensor or internal fault of the power drive unit

P0DF9.d: P0DF9 is stored when the C temperature sensor of the generator inverter reports a voltage at or beyond the upper end of its window. For the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi defines the limit as 3.75 V for 0.08 s on the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor, monitored continuously whenever the GCU has at least 8 V.
s: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature stuck at a very low value
Generator output held back
c: Open signal line of sensor C
Terminal pushed back in the inverter connector
Broken sensor element inside the power drive unit

P0DFA.d: In a three-phase machine the currents of phases U, V and W add up to nearly zero at every instant, so a sum far from zero shows that at least one current sensor is wrong. P0DFA is the code for this cross-check on the generator side.
s: Stop Safely Now or hybrid system warning
Vehicle may not start or ready mode is refused
Generator shut down, restricted driving
c: 12 V voltage drop at key-on (Ford SSM 50151)
One phase current sensor with offset or gain error
Internal fault of the inverter or power drive unit

P0DFB.d: The position sensor of a hybrid generator, normally a resolver, is never mounted exactly in line with the magnetic poles of the rotor. The remaining angle error is determined once and saved in the controller; Hyundai describes doing this after assembly and again whenever the machine or its control unit is replaced, and Ford describes an in-vehicle routine started by a scan tool that sweeps the current angle and reads
s: Hybrid system warning and engine warning light
Generator not used, reduced charging or engine start problems
Code returns after clearing until relearned
c: Offset learning interrupted or run under wrong conditions
Resolver rotor or stator shifted after repair or damage
Fault or wrong software in the generator control unit

P0DFC.d: P0DFC is stored when the controller has no valid learned position offset for the generator resolver. Ford explains it in the OBD summary of its power-split hybrids: the code appears when the resolver was not configured at the assembly plant or after the inverter system controller has been replaced, and the check fails if the value held in EEPROM is outside its accepted range.
s: Engine warning light on
Generator or hybrid functions restricted
Sometimes only stored as history code without symptoms
c: Inverter or hybrid controller replaced without resolver learning
Software fault in the inverter generator module (Volvo, update available)
Stored offset lost or corrupted in EEPROM

P0DFD.d: P0DFD flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of the valve that controls coolant flow through the on-board charger. Such a valve lets the thermal system send coolant to the charger during AC charging and bypass it while driving.
s: Charging slower than usual or interrupted
Charging or service message
Driving usually unaffected
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the valve
Open coil or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P0DFE.d: P0DFE means the control line of the charger coolant valve reads low, usually because it is shorted to ground somewhere between driver and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DFE publicly.
s: Reduced charging power, longer charging time
Charger warning or charging stops
Driving normally unaffected
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve actuator

P0DFF.d: P0DFF is the short-to-voltage case for the valve that cools the on-board charger. The controller sees the drive line high while commanding it low.
s: Charging slower or charger warning
Valve audibly running to its end stop
Driving normally unaffected
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the controlling module will not switch off
Internal fault in the valve actuator
